State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP09915-09
AGENCY DKT. NO. PERS #2- 797730
CYNTHIA WESLEY, ON REMAND
Petitioner, OAL DKT. NO.: TYP 11798-07
v.
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT
SYSTEM,
Respondent.
__________________________________
Jonathan S. Fabricant, Esq., for petitioner (Bathgate, Wegener and Wolf,
attorneys)
Danielle Bradus, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (Anne Milgram,
Attorney General of New Jersey, attorney)
Record Returned to OAL September 9, 2009 Decided: September 22, 2009
BEFORE CAROL I. COHEN, ALJ:
PROCEDURAL HISTORY AND STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The petitioner, Cynthia Wesley, filed an Application for Disability Retirement on February 1, 2007. In June 20, 2007, the Board of Trustees of the
Public Employees' Retirement System (PERS) denied the petitioner's application. The Board found that Ms. Wesley was not totally and
permanently disabled from the performance of her regular and assigned duties. However, with her age and/or years of service, she qualified for a
deferred retirement. On July 19, 2007, the petitioner, through counsel, sent a letter to the Secretary of the Board requesting that the matter be
referred to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) for a hearing. The Board approved the petitioner's request for an administrative hearing on
August 15, 2007.
The matter was filed with the OAL on November 13, 2007. A telephone pre-hearing conference was held on December 26, 2007. The matter
was originally scheduled for a hearing on July 16 and 17, 2008. The case was adjourned because the petitioner's expert had recently undergone
hip surgery. It was rescheduled for February 4 and 19, 2009. The February 4 date was adjourned because of the Judge's scheduling conflict. That
date was rescheduled to March 2, 2009. The matter was heard on February 19. However, the March date had to be adjourned because one of
the petitioner's expert witnesses was not available to testify. The matter was rescheduled for May 8, 2009, and heard on that date. Summation
briefs were received on July 6, 2009. An initial decision was issued on July 29, 2009. The PERS Board filed exceptions on August 11, 2009. On
August 20, 2009 the Board remanded the matter back to the ALJ for clarification as to whether the petitioner was totally and permanently
disabled from employment as of the date of her retirement. On September 17, 2009 I had a telephone conference with the attorneys for the
parties. They both agreed that no further submissions were necessary and my decision should be made by a review of the prior record.
ISSUE
Whether the petitioner was totally and permanently disabled from employment as of the date of her retirement?
FINDINGS OF FACT
See prior findings in July 29, 2009 Initial Decision

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The applicable statute that governs the case of Ordinary Disability states:
A member, under 60 years of age, who has 10 or more years of credit for New Jersey service, shall, upon the
application of the head of the department in which he shall have been employed or upon his own application or the
application of one acting in his behalf, be retired for ordinary disability by the board of trustees. The physician or
physicians designated by the board shall have first made a medical examination of him at his residence or at any
other place mutually agreed upon and shall have certified to the board that the member is physically or mentally
incapacitated for the performance of duty and should be retired.
[N.J.S.A. 43:15A-42 (emphasis added).]
In their exceptions the Board argued that:
Dr. Klemons testified that he discharged Petitioner asymptomatic from his care in December 2006, and could not
state whether or not Petitioner was disabled at that time. In July 2008, when Petitioner returned to Dr. Klemons, he
concluded that Petitioner was totally and permanently [disabled] from general secretarial work based on his
examination. This determination was made over a year after Petitioner applied for an ordinary disability retirement
in 2007 and long after Petitioner stopped working in January 2006.
Similarly, Dr. Othee, Petitioner's pain management specialist, testified that Petitioner left his care in February 2007,
even though he recommended a follow-up appointment in four weeks…..It is at this point, in July 2008, that Dr.
Othee opined that Petitioner is totally and permanently disabled. Thus, based on the competent, credible evidence
in the record, including the testimony of Petitioner's medical experts, Petitioner was not totally and permanently
disabled until July 2008.
I do not concur with the argument put forward by the Board. While it is true that in Dr. Klemons initial report he discharged the petitioner as
asymptomatic, he also made it clear in his testimony that it did not mean that the problem did not persist.
Dr. Klemons recounted that Mrs. Wesley Jackson first came to him on August 23, 2006, complaining of eye pain, blurred vision, pressure
in the ears, ear aches, jaw pain and fatigue, clicking sounds in her jaw, pain when chewing and yawning, sinus pain, dryness in the mouth, pain in
her teeth, shoulder, hand and back. . His working diagnosis of her condition was that she had experienced stretching and tearing in the mandibular
area with spasm and degenerative changes in the face, head and shoulders. She was experiencing headaches and facial pain, myositis, swallow
dysphasia, inflammatory arthritis, temporal tendonitis, limited mandibular range of motion. In addition the disc of the TMJ was dislocated and there
were joint changes as a result of trauma. It was Dr. Klemons opinion that the symptoms that Mrs. Wesley Jackson was experiencing were, to a
reasonable degree of medical probability, the result of the trauma that she had sustained in the automobile accident.
Dr. Klemons stated that he treated the petitioner until December 8, 2006, when she moved to Virginia. When asked about the limitations
that she claimed that she experienced as a result of the condition, he said that she stated that she had difficulty cleaning, standing, kneeling in
church, chewing gum and kissing. It also interfered with her ability to participate in sports and have normal sexual relations. She spent a lot of time
in bed and she felt extremely stressed. Dr. Klemons opined that these symptoms were consistent with the type of injuries that she had sustained.
His working diagnosis was that she had muscle stretching and tearing with spasm and degenerative changes in the face, head and shoulders. She
suffered from myalgia, headaches and facial pain, myositis, swallow dysphasia, inflammatory arthritis, temporal tendonitis, thoracic outlet
syndrome, limited mandibular range of motion, dislocation of the disc of the TMJ and joint changes as a result of trauma.
At the time that Mrs. Wesley Jackson moved to Virginia, Dr. Klemons had hoped that she would be able to maintain the improved
condition that he had seen prior to her leaving. He recommended that she try to wean herself from the device he had made for her. When she
attempted to do so her condition worsened as he reported when he saw her on July 15, 2008. Further, when he was queried about what had
changed between 2006 when he had discharged Mrs. Wesley Jackson from treatment as asymptomatic and now when he was stating that she was
permanently disabled, he testified that what had happened was that time had taken its toll. He might have been able to reduce her pain but her
problem i.e., muscle damage, spasm and degenerative changes to muscles, ligaments, tendons and joints of the head, face, neck and shoulders
persisted. The medications that she was taking masked her pain somewhat, but did not resolve the underlying condition.
Looking at Dr. Klemon's testimony in its totality it is clear that while Ms. Wesley Jackson's condition improved for a short period of time it was a
temporary cessation of a continuing deterioration caused by the motor vehicle accident. Her disabling condition continued to exist.
Dr. Othee, who testified as Mrs. Wesley Jackson's treating pain management physician, diagnosed her as having a chronic S-1 radiculopathy in her
low back causing pain and numbness in her back and neck and numbness and tingling down her right arm. He also noted reduced range of motion.
He testified that he had performed a number of diagnostic tests including an EMG to try to determine the cause of her pain. He stated that the
objective tests that he performed validated the subjective complaints that Mrs. Wesley Jackson had reported to him. On October 19, 2006, Mrs.
Wesley Jackson reported that her low-back pain was improved, but her range of motion was restricted and she was positive for leg raises on her
right side. Dr. Othee recommended a continuation of physical therapy and motrin for pain. In subsequent visits the petitioner reported an increase
in pain and Dr.Othee prescribed medication to alleviate the pain and muscle spasms. He continued to recommend that she not return to work
because of her pain and the side effects, including drowsiness caused by the medications that she was taking. When she returned on December 16,
2006 Mrs. Wesley Jackson reported no change in her level of pain. Similarly on January 11, 2007, she reported no change. The doctor

recommended continuing physical therapy and gave her lydoderm patches to manage her pain. There seem to have been no change in her level of
pain when she came to see Dr. Othee on February 15, 2007. Thus, at the time Mrs. Wesley Jackson filed her application for retirement, she was
suffering the same symptoms that she continued to report to Dr. Othee. While her condition continued to deteriorate, as Dr. Othee reported when
he saw her in July 2008, about sixteen months later, it is clear that the same problem, that had caused Dr. Othee to recommend that she continue in
treatment and not return to work, had persisted. Even though she sought medical treatment when she moved to Virginia, her condition did not
improve, in fact it became worse. Dr. Othee viewed her symptoms as being chronic and recommended that she not sit, bend, stand or walk for
prolonged periods of time. This was a continuation of his recommendation from 2006 and 2007, when he ordered that she not return to work,
because she could not perform the normal duties of a secretary.
CONCLUSION
Based on the above findings of fact and analysis of the law, I CONCLUDE that the petitioner was permanently disabled from the
performance of her duties at the time she initially filed for retirement benefits on February 1, 2007 and is therefore entitled to ordinary disability
benefits from that date forward.
ORDER
It is hereby ORDERED that the petitioner's application for disability retirement benefits is hereby GRANTED effective February 1,
2007.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM for
consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES'
RETIREMENT SYSTEM, which by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees'
Retirement System does not adopt, modify or reject this decision within forty-five days and unless such time limit is otherwise extended, this
recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
Within thirteen days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written exceptions with the
DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF PENSIONS, One State Street Square, 50 West State Street, P.O. Box 295, Trenton, New Jersey
08625-0295, marked "Attention: Exceptions." A copy of any exceptions must be sent to the judge and to the other parties.

DIANE CRUM,
Petitioner,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMENS'
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
______________________________
George T. Daggett, Esq., for petitioner
(Daggett, Kraemer & Eliades, attorneys)
David Skand, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent
(John J. Farmer, Jr., Attorney General of New Jersey, Attorney)
Record Closed: September 30, 1999 Decided: October 1, 1999
BEFORE R. JACKSON DWYER, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Petitioner, Diane Crum, appeals from the determination of respondent, the Board of Trustees of the Police and Firemen's Retirement System
(The Board, PFRS), at its meeting of September 15, 1997 denying her request for an accidental disability retirement allowance, pursuant to
N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. The Board determined that the incident on December 11, 1995 was not a “traumatic event,” pursuant to statute and case law.
By letter dated September 24, 1997, petitioner requested a hearing, and by letter dated October 23, 1997, the Board approved petitioner's
request to appeal its September 15, 1997 decision. This matter was transmitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) by the Division of
Pensions on October 23, 1997, for hearing as a contested case pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to -15 and N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -13. The hearing
was held on September 14, 1999. Posthearing submissions were received by the administrative law judge (ALJ) from petitioner on September 18
and from respondent on September 30, 1999.
STIPULATIONS
The parties agreed to the following stipulations:
1. Petitioner, Diane Crum, was born on October 2, 1958 (J-2).
2. Petitioner obtained employment with the County of Sussex, State of New Jersey, on June 24, 1986 (J-2).
3. Petitioner received a permanent appointment as a County Correction Officer on December 18, 1989 (J-2).
4. As a result of this appointment, petitioner was enrolled in the Police and Firemen's Retirement System (PFRS) (J-2).
5. Petitioner has a total of 5 years and 11 months of PFRS service credit. She was employed as a Sussex County Correction Officer until
January 31, 1997, when she resigned (J-3).
6. On December 18, 1996, petitioner executed an Application for an Accidental Disability Retirement Allowance, requesting an effective
retirement date of June 1, 1996. Petitioner claimed that she was totally and permanently disabled as a result of an incident which occurred on
December 11, 1995 (J-3).
7. At its regular meeting on September 15, 1997, the PFRS Board denied petitioner's application for an Accidental Disability Retirement
Allowance. The Board found that petitioner was totally and permanently disabled from the performance of her regular and assigned duties, but her

disability was not the direct result of the incident on December 11, 1995, and that that incident was not a “traumatic event” pursuant to statute and
court decisions. The Board, therefore, granted petitioner an Ordinary Disability Retirement Allowance (J-4).
8. By letter dated September 24, 1997, petitioner's counsel appealed the Board's decision denying her an Accidental Disability Retirement
Allowance). (J-5).
9. At its regular meeting on October 20, 1997, the PFRS Board approved the petitioner's request for a hearing. The Board determined the
matter was a contested case pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 et seq. and N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 et seq., and transmitted the matter to the Office of
Administrative Law on October 23, 1997 (J-6).
10. At its meeting of March 3, 1999, the PFRS Board reconsidered this matter, and determined that petitioner's disability was the direct result of
the incident that occurred on December 11, 1995. The Board reaffirmed its decision that the incident itself was not a traumatic event.
THE TESTIMONY
On December 11, 1995, petitioner, Diane Crum, was assigned to work at the command center of the Keough-Dwyer Correctional Facility in
Sussex County. Inmate Robert Gilligan in Cell 207 became violent and his obscenities were heard by petitioner through the ceiling vents. Petitioner
observed inmate Gilligan smear toothpaste on the window of his cell. Petitioner notified a supervisor on the first floor about the commotion. That
sergeant told petitioner to have correction officers Donald Ziolkowski and Edward Nemeth calm the inmate down. The correction officers went to
the inmate's cell. Petitioner, who remained at the command center, unlocked the inmates' door. Petitioner observed that the inmate was punching
and kicking. The correction officers requested assistance to subdue the inmate. Petitioner called correction officer Blagec to assist the correction
officers; however, he failed to arrive. Petitioner left the command center to help the correction officers subdue the inmate. Petitioner entered the
inmate's cell and observed correction officers Ziolkowski and Nemeth were trying to cuff the inmate. The correction officers told petitioner to get
the leg shackles. Petitioner returned to the command center and got the leg shackles; she reentered the inmate's cell and observed he was kicking,
spitting and trying to bite the correction officers. Correction officers Ziolkowski and Nemeth attempted to restrain the inmate's upper body while
she laid across the inmate to shackle his legs together.
As petitioner laid across the inmate's legs, he “lifted” her up with one of his legs and propelled her into the wall. Correction officer Blagec
arrived and shackled the inmate's legs after petitioner had returned to the command center.
Cross examination focused on the written statements of the incident. Petitioner testified that she filled out a “Report of Misconduct or Other
Incident” a couple of hours after the incident. She wrote:
While I was helping C.O. Blagec shackle inmate Gilligan's legs, he was kicking and thrashing his legs violently therefore making my back strain.
She also wrote on her report:
. . . C. O. Blagec entered Cell 207 and was kicked in the ribs by inmate Gilligan . . .
Petitioner filed a Workers' Compensation Claim Form (R-2), with the Division of Personnel on December 11, 1995 and wrote how the injury
occurred:
I was helping fellow officers shackling legs together. The inmate was violent and resisting, therefore, I hurt my back.
Sergeant Demchak submitted a “Supervisors Accident Investigation Report,” dated December 13, 1995 (R-3). He wrote:
(Petitioner) hurt back while helping to shackle inmate.
Petitioner filled out an Application for Accidental Disability Retirement, dated December 18, 1996. Question 7 on the application reads: I
declare I am incapacitated for further service as a correction officer due to the following reasons:
Petitioner wrote:
On December 11, 1995, I was attacked by a male inmate at the Sussex County Jail. I have suffered a permanent back injury.
Petitioner stated she has never prepared a written statement that she had been lifted off one of inmate Gilligan's legs and propelled into a wall.
Petitioner had back surgery for a herniated disc in 1990 and reinjured her back in 1993 when she fell on a wet floor in the print room.
ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The choice of accepting or rejecting the testimony of the witness rests with me, the initial trier and finder of the facts. I must make a reasonable
choice. Hornauer v. Division of Alcoholic Beverage Control, 40 N.J. Super. 501, 506 (App. Div. 1956). The question the ALJ has wrestled
with is why petitioner would omit from her Report of Misconduct or Other Incident (R-1), prepared while she was under the influence of the
event, that she was lifted off of one of the inmate's legs and propelled into a wall, if the accident had, in fact, happened that way. Petitioner wrote in
her report that correction officer Blagec had been kicked in the ribs by the inmate, but she only reported that she suffered a back sprain. Likewise,
the Worker's Compensation Claim Form, the Supervisor's Accident Investigation Report, and her Application for Accidental Disability
Retirement all neglect to mention petitioner's version of how the accident happened at the hearing.

Turning to the three prongs in Kane v. Bd. of Trustees of the Police and Firemens'' Retirement System, 100 N.J. 651 (1985), I FIND that:
1. Petitioner suffered a back strain on the date of the incident which was induced by the stress and strain of the normal work effort;
2. Petitioner met involuntarily with the source or object that was the source of harm;
3. Petitioner's testimony strains credulity. Petitioner's written report, prepared two hours after the incident, is how her injury occurred.
Petitioner strained her back trying to subdue the inmate. A back strain is not a traumatic event because it does not involve “a great rush of force or
uncontrollable power.” Mazza v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemens' Retirement System, 143 N.J. 22 (1995).
For the foregoing reasons, I CONCLUDE petitioner did not sustain a “traumatic event” on December 11, 1995 and therefore is not entitled to
an accidental disability retirement allowance under N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. Petitioner's application IS DENIED. IT IS SO ORDERED.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN'S RETIREMENT SYSTEM
for consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND
FIREMEN'S RETIREMENT SYSTEM who by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of Trustees of the Police
and Firemen's Retirement System does not adopt, modify or reject this decision within forty-five (45) days and unless such time limit is otherwise
extended, this recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
Within thirteen (13) days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written exceptions
with the DIRECTOR, DIVISION OF PENSIONS, One State Street Square, 50 West State Street, PO Box 295, Trenton, New Jersey
08625-0295, marked "Attention: Exceptions." A copy of any exceptions must be sent to the judge and to the other parties.

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP9896-97
AGENCY DKT. NO. PERS 251994
MICHAEL CORTESE,
Petitioner
v.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC
EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
________________________________
Andrew Bayer, Esq., for petitioner
(DeCotiis, Fitzpatrick & Gluck, attorneys)
Kimberly A. Sked, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent
(James J. Farmer, Jr., Attorney General of New Jersey, attorney)
Record Closed: April 16, 1999 Decided: July 27, 1999
BEFORE IRENE JONES, ALJ:
Petitioner, Michael Cortese, appeals the April 20, 1997 decision of the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees' Retirement System (PERS
or Board) that found $63,685 of compensation as extracurricular in nature and thus not pensionable. On September 17, 1997, petitioner filed a
notice of appeal with the PERS. The matter was transmitted by the PERS on October 23, 1997 to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL) for
hearing as a contested case pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to 14F-1.
A plenary hearing was scheduled on August 14, 1998 and was adjourned at the request of the respondent. The matter was rescheduled for
March 11, 1999 and was heard on that date. The parties submitted post hearing submissions and the record closed on April 16, 1999. At the
request of the undersigned the time for the issuance of the initial decision was extended by the Director of the Department of the Treasury until July
15, 1999.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the record, I FIND the following FACTS:
Michael C. Cortese, C.P.A., the petitioner (petitioner or Cortese) was born on September 28, 1945. He is 53 years old. He was enrolled in the
Public Employees' Retirement System on February 2, 1970, with deductions beginning on April 1, 1970 (J-2).
From 1980 to 1986, petitioner was the Controller for the Essex County Finance Department and from 1986 to 1996, he served as Auditor to
the Essex County Board of Chosen Freeholders. He was also a principal of M.C. Cortese & Associates, an accounting firm he founded in 1977
(P-1).
In 1992, the Essex County Utilities Authority (ECUA) was formed, inter alia, to provide for the County's solid waste management needs. The
petitioner assisted in its formation and continued to provide accounting and consulting services to the ECUA through his accounting firm. In 1995,
by resolution, the ECUA established the position of Director of Finance and Administration (P-3). According to the resolution, the Director of
Finance and Administration would perform:
such tasks and duties as are required to (I) establish and implement a system of financial management, (ii) administer the Authority's contracts, (iii)
administer the Authority's project financing documents, and (iv) perform such other tasks and duties as are required from time to time and as shall
be assigned by the Chairman of the Authority, the Chairman of the Finance and Budget Committee and/or the Executive Director, as the case may
be. Such duties and responsibilities shall be substantially similar to the tasks previously undertaken on behalf of the Authority by M.C. Cortese &
Associates, in its capacity as financial advisor to the Authority.
On October 15, 1995, petitioner signed a five-year Employment Agreement with the ECUA to fill the position (J-3) His duties were described
in an Employment Agreement as follows:
Section 1. Duties. (a) During the term of this contract, EMPLOYEE shall, among other things, perform those duties and services previously
performed by the ECUA's outside financial consultant, M.C. Cortese & Associates. In such capacity, among other things, EMPLOYEE shall (a)
perform such tasks and duties as are required to establish and implement a system of financial management, (b) administer the ECUA's contracts
and financing documents, and (c) perform such other tasks and duties as are required from time to time and as shall be assigned by the Chairman

of the ECUA, the Chairman of the Finance and Budget Committee and/or the Executive Director, as the case may be. EMPLOYEE shall also
supervise and direct all employees of, and advisors, consultants and other contractors to ECUA with respect to all financial and related matters.
(b) In addition to the duties and responsibilities to be perform by EMPLOYEE as Director of Finance and Administration hereunder, during any
period that the Executive Director is not able to perform his duties, EMPLOYEE shall exercise such powers and carry out such responsibilities as
are properly exercised by the Executive Director.
(c) EMPLOYEE agrees that he will at all times faithfully, industriously, and to the best of his ability, experience and talents, perform all of the duties
that may be required of and from him pursuant to the express and implicit terms of this Agreement, such duties shall be rendered at the ECUA's
principal office and at such other place or places as ECUA shall in good faith require or as the interest, needs, business or opportunity of ECUA
shall require.
Petitioner's base compensation was set forth in the Employment Agreement and provided as follows:
Section 4. Compensation. (a) Base Compensation. As and for all full compensation for the services to be provided by EMPLOYEE hereunder,
during the period from the effective date of this Agreement to and including December 31, 1995, EMPLOYEE shall be compensated on an hourly
basis for the actual amount of hours of service provided by EMPLOYEE (as evidenced by time records which shall be maintained by
EMPLOYEE and submitted to ECUA), calculated on the basis of an annual salary of $89,000.
The employment agreement also provided for additional compensation opportunities, reading in pertinent part:
(2) In the event that the ECUA undertakes any financing (either through the issuance of short-term project notes or long-term revenues bonds)
for or with respect to the Solid Waste System during the term of this Agreement, EMPLOYEE shall (in consideration for services provided in
support thereof), receive additional compensation (payable at the closing for such project notes or bonds) in a fixed amount equal to $1.00 per
$1,000 principal amount of project notes or revenue bonds issued.
Thus, under the terms of the agreement, petitioner as Director of Finance and Administration, was entitled to hourly compensation based on an
annual $89,000 salary. Additionally, should the ECUA undertake any debt financing pursuant to section 4(b)(2) of the employment agreement,
petitioner was entitled to $1.00 per $1,000 of the debt for his undefined, financing - related services.
Petitioner provided financing-related services to the ECUA from December 1995 to April 1996, when the ECUA issued solid waste long-term
revenue bonds in the amount of $63,685,000. He received a $63,685 commission for the bond issue, in accordance with the employment
agreement.
On or abut July 23, 1997, an accountant with the Division of Pensions and Benefits (“Division”) wrote to the petitioner advising him that his
$63,685 commission was not creditable compensation for pension purposes, and therefore the appropriate contributions would be refunded (J-4).
Thereafter, petitioner pursued an appeal at the Board (J-5). On August 20, 1997, the Board determined that the petitioner's commission was non-
creditable compensation, pursuant to the definition of “compensation” in N.J.S.A. 43:15A-6(r) (J-6).
In February 1998, petitioner and the ECUA entered into an amended and restated employment agreement, extending his term of employment
until December 2000. However, the ECUA terminated the employment relationship because the ECUA's role was diminished as a result of a
decision by the Third Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlantic Coast Demolition and Recycling, Inc. v. Board of Chosen Freeholders of Atlantic
County, 112 F.3d 652 (3rd Cir. 1997). In that decision, the Department of Environmental Protection was enjoined from implementing its solid
waste self-sufficiency policy, thereby enabling out-of-state waste disposal facilities to compete with in-state facilities. In any event, the latter
agreement is irrelevant to this matter, since it was subsequent to the denial of pensionability.
TESTIMONY
Petitioner testified as to his qualifications and educational background (P-1). In addition to being a Certified Public Accountant, petitioner is
certified as a Municipal and County Finance Officer. Prior to working with the ECUA, petitioner was employed by the Essex County Prosecutor's
office as a Supervising Auditor/Investigator. In 1980 he became the County Controller and Chief Financial Officer in the Essex County Finance
Department. He served in this capacity from 1980 to 1986. In 1986, petitioner was employed by the County Board of Chosen Freeholders as an
Internal Auditor. He left that position to assume and become an independent contractor with the newly-formed ECUA as its Chief Financial
Officer (CFO). His duties were to develop a budget and a business plan. He was responsible for all financial matters submitted to the Authority.
The petitioner was also the ECUA's financial advisor. Petitioner asserts that his duties in the latter capacity was distinguishable from his duties as
the CFO. Specifically, as a Financial Advisor he was required to deal with financing, procurements and financing for bonds and notes. From 1992
to 1995, the ECUA undertook several financing wherein long term revenue bonds of $63,685,000 were issued. Petitioner provided financing
related services for the issuance and pursuant to Section 2 of the employment Agreement he was paid a commission of $63,685. Petitioner asserts
that he provided the following services:
determined the amount, size, timing and frequency of borrowing necessary to provide for the ECUA's solid waste system;
assessed credit structure, maturity schedule, call provisions and other items, as required;
prepared necessary legal and financial documents concerning debt transactions;

examined various debt financing alternatives, including variable rate debt, interest rate swaps and other derivative products (if and when they
become feasible under State statutes);
prepared official statements, including ongoing updating of demographic data and financial statistic included therein;
presented information on proposed financing in the ECUA's finances and operations to the Bond Rating agencies;
evaluated the terms and recommendations to ECUA of acceptance, rejection or renegotiation with respect to sale bids or final pricing;
assessed matters related to the settlement and delivery of bonds and notes;
prepared information on proposed financing to institutions providing credit enhancement and potential investments;
developed comprehensive financing plans for ECUA as well as specific plans to assist staff with on-going operations;
As CFO his duties were to:
assisted the ECUA members in the preparation of the annual budget;
supervise the posting and maintenance of all books regarding the entry of all funds;
compliance with DCA statutes and regulations;
supervise the preparation of monthly reports for the Treasurer;
compliance with Single Audit Requirements;
supervision of petty cash and change funds
preparation and signing of Annual Financial Statement, Annual Debt Statement and Supplemental Debt Statement;
coordination of bank reconciliation's;
custody of all public funds; and
preparation of end of fiscal year reports.
The ECUA issued one revenue bond and thus petitioner admits that he did not receive any additional compensation as a financial advisor.
Donald Biase (Biase), a former ECUA Commissioner and Chairman of the Finance and Budget Committee, testified that on behalf of the
ECUA he negotiated the Employment Agreement with the petitioner. It was his understanding that the petitioner's position as CFO was
distinguishable from his position as the ECUA's Financial Advisor. Biase testified as to different requirements of the both positions. He further
noted that the Employment Agreement (J-3) envisioned two separate functions and sought to account for the two functions. Specifically, the
ECUA did not want to put petitioner's compensation as Financial advisor in his salary. In his view, a Financial Advisor is not generally the CFO.
Indeed one would not want to overlap the two positions.
ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
At issue is whether the $63,685 of compensation paid to the petitioner is creditable for pension purposes.
The Board contends that the income was outside of the petitioner's base salary, thus it is extra income and therefore not pensionable. Petitioner
argues that this income was pursuant to the Employment Agreement, salary for work done as a part and parcel of his position as Financial Advisor.
The compensation was not extracurricular and this position is based on a misunderstanding of the petitioner's job functions. Specifically, petitioner
contends that he performed two distinct jobs, CFO and Financial Advisor, thus he is entitled to compensation and pension credit for each position.
Rokos v. State, Dept. of Treasury, 236 N.J. Super. 174 (App. Div. 1989).
The term compensation is defined by the Public Employees' Retirement Act,
N.J.S.A. 43:15A-1 et seq., as
the base or contractual salary, for services as an employee, which is in accordance with established salary policies of the member's employer for all
employees in the same position but shall not include individual salary adjustments which are granted primarily in anticipation of the member's
retirement or additional remuneration for performing temporary or extracurricular duties beyond the regular work day or the regular work year. In
cases where salary includes maintenance, the retirement system shall fix the value of that part of the salary not paid in money which shall be
considered under this act.
[N.J.S.A. 43:15A-6(r).]
Compensation and salary are deemed synonymous for pension credit purposes. Chapel v. Board of Trustees of Public Employees' Retirement
System, 258 N.J. Super 389, 393 (App. Div. 1992) (citing Fasolo v. Board of Trustees, 181 N.J. Super 434 (App. Div. 1981), wherein salary
is defined as moneys received by a person on a fixed and continuous basis, i.e., normally paid in regular periodic intervals in specific dollar
amounts). Id., quoting Koribanics v. Board of Educ., 48 N.J 1, 6 (1966). A pension member's base or contractual salary is creditable for
retirement benefits, but his or her “extra compensation” is not. N.J.A.C. 17:2-4.1(d) provides examples of extra compensation as:
overtime, bonus, longevity lump sum payments, individual retroactive salary adjustments or individual adjustments to place a member at maximum
in his salary range in the final year of service, increments granted for retirement credit in recognition of the member's forthcoming retirement or in
recognition of the member's years of service in the community.

The Court has consistently held that a member holding two positions is entitled to pension credit for compensation received from both positions.
See Siri v. Board of Trustees of Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund, 262 N.J. Super 147 (App. Div. 1993) (teacher appointed as
department chairperson entitled to pension credit for both positions); Chapel v. Board of Trustees of Public Employees' Retirement System,
Div. of Pensions, 258 N.J. Super 389 (App. Div. 1992) (supervisor of buildings and grounds appointed as clerk of the works entitled to pension
credit for both positions); Hiering v. Board of Trustees of Public Employees Retirement System, Div. of Pensions, Dept. of Treasury, 197
N.J. Super 14 (App. Div. 1984) (general counsel of utilities authority appointed as municipal prosecutor of borough entitled to pension credit for
both positions); Fasolo v. Bd, of Trustees, 6 N.J.A.R. 4 (Div. of Pensions 1980), rev'd in part, 181 N.J. Super. 434 (App. Div. 1981)
(magistrate appointed as sewer attorney entitled to pension credit for both positions); Rokos v. State, Dept. of Treasury, Div. of Pensions, 236
N.J. Super 174 (App. Div. 1989) (municipal court judge appointed as presiding judge entitled to pension credit for both positions).
In Rokos, supra, the petitioner therein, a municipal court judge, was appointed presiding judge of the vicinage in conjunction with a Supreme
Court pilot project. He spent three days a week as presiding judge, performing various administrative and extra-municipal judicial duties, and two
days a week as a municipal court judge. Upon retirement, he sought pension credit for compensation he received from both positions. The Board
denied his request on the basis that his presiding judge salary constituted additional compensation beyond his base salary. The Appellate Division
reversed, both the Board and the ALJ finding, inter alia, that a municipal court judgeship was a separate and independent appointment from a
presiding judgeship and was therefore entitled to separate pension credit. Id. at 183.
Petitioner asserts that Rokos is controlling herein. The Board asserts that the pivotal distinction between Rokos and the present matter is that the
petitioner herein was appointed to one position, Director of Finance and Administration, with duties that were broad and non-specific,
encompassing those of a CFO, Financial Advisor, and a number of other roles.
As noted above, the petitioner and former Commissioner Biase testified that it was intended for the petitioner to be the CFO and Financial
Advisor to the ECUA upon his appointment. However, this intent is not evinced anywhere in the employment agreement. See Casriel v. King, 2
N.J 45, 51 (1948) (extrinsic evidence showing an intention wholly unexpressed in the writing is irrelevant).
Under the employment agreement, as Director of Finance and Administration, petitioner was required to perform the following duties: (1)
establish and implement a system of financial management; (2) administer the ECUA's contracts and financing documents; (3) perform “such other
tasks and duties as are required from time to time and as shall be assigned by the Chairman of the ECUA, the Chairman of the Finance and Budget
Committee and/or the Executive Director”; (4) supervise and direct all employees, advisors, consultants, and other contractors to the ECUA with
respect to all financial and related matters; (5) fill in for the Executive Director, if necessary; and (6) perform “all of the duties that may be required
of and from him pursuant to the express and implicit terms” of the employment agreement. He was entitled to hourly compensation as Director of
Finance and Administration based on an annual $89,000 salary. This compensation, according to the employment agreement, constituted “all full
compensation”.
It was only in the event that the ECUA undertook debt financing by issuing short-term project notes or long-term revenue bonds, that the
petitioner was entitled to additional compensation, in a fixed amount. These services were undefined. No distinction is made in the text of the
employment agreement regarding petitioner's distinct roles as CFO or Financial Advisor. On the contrary, implicit in the petitioner's responsibilities
as the Director of Finance and Administration was to provide financial advisory duties to the ECUA and fiscal management duties similar to those
of a CFO. In other words, even if the ECUA did not engage in debt financing, the petitioner was required under the employment agreement to
provide financial advisory duties to the ECUA as it Director of Finance and Administration. The petitioner's premise implies the opposite, that he
was a Financial Advisor to the ECUA only with respect to the debt financing.
The term “compensation” as defined by the Public Employees' Retirement Act excludes additional remuneration for performing temporary or
extracurricular duties beyond the regular work day or the regular work year. N.J.S.A. 43:15A-6(r). Thus, neither additional remuneration for
performing temporary duties beyond the regular work day or work year nor additional remuneration for performing extracurricular duties beyond
the regular work day or work year is creditable compensation for pension purposes. In the Chapel case, supra, the Appellate Division held that
the term “extracurricular duties” encompasses “incidental additional services directly related to the basic employment.” Chapel, supra, 258 N.J.
Super. at 394, stated another way, these extracurricular duties must be functionally related to the basic duties. See Chapel, supra, 258 N.J.
Super. at 395-396 (citing Fasolo, supra, 181 N.J. Super. at 444). The legislative intent of this exception to the definition of compensation was to
prohibit creditability for overtime, special assignments, and the like. Rokos, supra, 236 N.J. Super. at 179.
I FIND that the petitioner's financing-related activities were incidental additional duties directly (i.e. functionally) related to his basic duties as
Director of Finance and Administration. As Director of Finance and Administration, petitioner was required by the employment agreement to
administer the ECUA's contracts and projects financing documents, perform those duties and services previously performed by the ECUA's
outside financial consultant, M.C. Cortese & Associates, and supervise and direct all employees of and advisors, consultants and other contractors
to ECUA with respect to all financial and related matters. Those were his basic duties. He was required to perform those basic duties pursuant to
the express and implicit terms of the employment agreement. He was also required to provide undefined support duties in connection with the
ECUA's debt financing. Thus, the petitioner's duties in support of the ECUA's debt financing, for which he received additional compensation in the
form of a $63,685 commission, were functionally related to his basic duties as Director of Finance and Administration. Indeed, it can only be
concluded that the petitioner's duties in support of the ECUA's debt financing were so functionally related to his basic duties, that the drafters of the
employment agreement did not consider it necessary to define his debt financing-related duties.
Furthermore, petitioner's financing-related duties were incidental to his basic duties. The petitioner quotes from the Webster's Dictionary
definition of “incidental” as “occurring merely by chance or with intention or calculation.” Under this definition, his debt financing-related duties
could not be considered incidental, as these duties were clearly anticipated in the employment agreement. Under the legal definition of “incidental”,
however, “[d]epending upon or appertaining to something else as primary”, it is evident that the petitioner's debt financing-related duties
appertained to his primary (i.e., basic) duties as Director of Finance and Administration. Black's Law Dictionary 686 5th Ed. (1979).

The next issue is whether the petitioner's duties were extracurricular duties as defined in N.J.S.A. 43:15A.6(r). If the extracurricular duties to be
excluded were performed during the regular work day, the duties do not fall under the exception. Rather, the compensation earned from the
performance of the extracurricular duties during the regular work day are creditable for pension purposes. See Siri, supra, 262 N.J. Super. at
151.
Pursuant to the employment agreement, petitioner was required to work a minimum of 17 hours per week during regular business hours. He did
not have a 9 to 5 schedule or a regular work day or regular work year. In fact, petitioner essentially determined his own regular work day (within
the parameters of ECUA's regular business hours). Thus, the petitioner defined his own regular work day as Director of Finance and
Administration, and billed the ECUA on an hourly basis. Petitioner did not bill the ECUA for the time he spent on the bond financing-related
activities. Instead, he received a commission of $1 per $1,000 of the principal amount of the bonds issued, for a total of $63,685.
I FIND that petitioner performed his financing-related extracurricular duties beyond the regular work day. I therefore CONCLUDE that,
consistent with case law, compensation for extracurricular duties beyond the regular work day is not creditable compensation for pension
purposes, pursuant to N.J.S.A. 43:15A-6(r).
Finally, I FIND persuasive the Board's argument that the petitioner's $63,685 commission should not be credited as a matter of public policy.
The Board asserts that a public employee with a vested interest in maximizing the debt incurred by his employer “presents the potential for abuses
and impaired judgment”, and therefore, such compensation arrangements should not yield pension benefits. The petitioner argues that the
Commissioners of the ECUA approved the 1996 bond issue, and petitioner had no independent decision-making authority, and this lack of
independent decision-making authority negates any conflict.
A conflict of interest exists where contradictory desires tug a public official in opposite directions. See Wyzkowski v. Rizas, 132 N.J 509, 524
(1993) (citing LaRue v. Township of East Brunswick, 68 N.J. Super 435, 448 (App. Div. 1961)). Accordingly, the Local Government Ethics
Law, N.J.S.A. 40A:9-22.1 et seq., prohibits local government officers or employees from undertaking “any employment or service, whether
compensated or not, which might reasonably be expected to prejudice his independence of judgment in the exercise of his official duties.” N.J.S.A.
40A:9-22.5(e). In enacting the law, the Legislature made the following findings: public office and employment are a public trust; the stability of
representative democracy depends upon the public's confidence in the integrity of its public officials; and whenever the public perceives a conflict
between the private interests and the public duties of a government officer or employee, that confidence is imperiled. N.J.S.A. 40A:9-22.2(a), (c).
The Local Government Ethics Law demands that officers or employees discharge their duties with undivided loyalty. MacDougall v. Weivhert,
144 N.J. 380, 401 (1996).
In his capacity as Director of Finance and Administration, petitioner owed a fiduciary duty to the ECUA, and by extension, its constituents. “[A]
public officer assumes the same fiduciary relationship toward the citizens of his community as a trustee bears to his cestui que trust.” Aldom v.
Borough of Roseland, 42 N.J. Super 495, 501 (App. Div. 1956)(citation omitted). Petitioner was the equivalent of a trustee who advised the
beneficiary on a mortgage of the trust res while collecting a commission on the mortgage. He supervised the ECUA's financial record-keeping,
prepared the financial statements, held custody of the public funds, and advised the ECUA on “the amount, size, timing and frequency of
borrowing necessary to provide for the ECUA's solid waste system”. At the same time, he received compensation in direct proportion to the
amount of that borrowing. His pecuniary self-interest in maximizing the debt incurred by the ECUA, and ultimately, its constituents, was
incompatible with his fiduciary duties. “No man, much less a public fiduciary, can sit on both sides of a bargaining table. He cannot in one capacity
pass with undivided loyalty upon proposals he advances in his other role.” McDonough v. Roach, 39 N.J 418, 156 (1961).
Notably, petitioner became the Director of Finance and Administration of the ECUA on October 15, 1995. Petitioner was also the Auditor to
the Essex County Board of Chosen Freeholders until 1996. Moreover, petitioner began advising the ECUA on its debt financing in December
1995. Thus, for a period of time, petitioner was advising the ECUA on the bond issue, which he stood to personally profit from in proportion to its
amount, while serving as a fiduciary to the ECUA and the Essex County Board of Chosen Freeholders and its constituents, who were ultimately
liable for the bond issue. See footnote 1 In April 1996, the ECUA issued solid waste long-term revenue bonds in the amount of $63,685,000, and
the petitioner received a $63,685 commission. Had he advised the ECUA to issue bonds for half that amount, and the Commissioners followed his
professional advice, his commission would have been cut in half. The incentive to maximize the ECUA's debt is obvious.
I FIND and CONCLUDE that the petitioner's pecuniary interest in maximizing the debt incurred by the ECUA was incompatible with his
fiduciary duties as the Director of Finance and Administration, the potential for conflict was palpable and, therefore, the Board should not credit his
$63,685 commission to his retirement benefits.
I hereby AFFIRM the Board's denial of pension credit for the $63,685 commission.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM for
consideration.

State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP 9736-12
AGENCY DKT. NO.
JOHN WEINLEIN,
Petitioner,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMEN’S
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
__________________________
John D. Feeley, Esq., petitioner
Jeremy M. Vaida, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (John J. Hoffman, Acting Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: June 27, 2014 Decided: November 10, 2014
BEFORE ROBERT BINGHAM II, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Petitioner John Weinlein appeals a denial of accidental disability retirement benefits on grounds that the traumatic event was not
undesigned and unexpected. On July 27, 2011, petitioner filed an application for disability retirement due to work-related injuries
sustained on December 20, 2009. On May 14, 2012, respondent, the Board of Trustees of the Police and Firemen’s Retirement
System (the Board or PFRS), denied petitioner’s application for accidental disability benefits and approved ordinary disability
instead. Petitioner filed a timely appeal and the matter was transmitted to the Office of Administrative Law (OAL), where it was

filed on July 18, 2012. N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to 15; N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -13. The hearing was held on May 19, 2014, and the
record remained open for post-hearing submissions. The record closed on June 27, 2014, upon receipt of the final post-hearing
submission, and extensions were granted until November 10, 2014, for issuance of this decision.
FACTUAL DISCUSSION
Weinlein was enrolled in the PFRS on or about September 21, 1979.( J-2.) In December 2009 he was chief of police of
the Township of Berkeley. The pertinent civil-service job specification for police chief (J-5) lists his duties including, for example,
provision of assistance for traffic emergencies.
On December 20, 2009, Weinlein injured his left arm and shoulder when, in the performance of his duties, he pushed the
rear of a snow-stuck car that lurched forward and caused him to fall. (P-1.) Consequently, on July 27, 2011, he filed an
application for accidental disability retirement based upon the injury. (J-3.) On May 14, 2012, the PFRS denied petitioner’s
application for accidental disability benefits, but approved ordinary disability. Specifically, the Board determined that the
petitioner was totally and permanently disabled from the performance of his regular and assigned duties, and that he was
physically or mentally incapacitated from the performance of his usual or other duties that his employer was willing to offer. The
Board also specifically determined that the causal event: (1) was identifiable as to time and place; (2) was caused by a
circumstance external to petitioner and was not the result of pre-existing disease; (3) occurred during and as a result of his
regular and assigned duties; and (4) did not involve an injury resulting from willful negligence. The Board based its denial upon a
determination that the incident that caused petitioner’s disability claim was not undesigned and unexpected. (J-6.) I FIND as
FACT the above undisputed evidence.
John Weinlein testified that on December 22, 2009, as police chief of Berkeley Township, he was involved with a work-
related accident while assisting with the removal of a vehicle from a snow embankment. He had responded to a call to assist a
woman who had a scheduled medical procedure, but whose car was stuck in the snow. As he assisted by pushing the rear of the
vehicle, rocking it back and forth, the car suddenly lurched forward, causing him to fall to the ground. (P-1; P-2.) He assumes the
driver had hit the gas pedal because the wheels were spinning when the car lurched forward. He landed on his left arm,
impacting his left shoulder. Though he had performed such service many times before, never had he encountered such an
occurrence. But for the accident, he would have continued to work until retirement at age sixty-five.
On cross-examination, Weinlein testified that, over the course of thirty-two years, he had assisted people with getting out
of the snow on ten to fifteen occasions. Though he was familiar with pushing cars, and had pushed perhaps one hundred cars,
including in conditions of mud and snow, nothing like this had ever happened before. He had experienced cars unable to escape
such an area, with acceleration of the gas, but never an incident when a car lurched forward like that.
In his experience, car wheels can spin upon acceleration when stuck in snow, but usually when the wheels are spinning,
the car does not escape that situation, though it may ultimately do so. In his experience, a car is usually freed by a front tow,
placement of something under it, or other ways that are not abrupt as occurred here. On this occasion, he did not place blocks
under the wheels and, if anything, would have used something that would create friction, like a rug.
Based upon the testimony and exhibits, as well as the opportunity to observe the appearance and demeanor of the witness, I
further FIND the following as FACT:
In the performance of his duties as police chief, petitioner had knowledge and experience regarding the removal of motor
vehicles from entrapment in snow. On numerous occasions he had assisted with such maneuvers, including the pushing of
vehicles. In his experience, even when car wheels spin in snow, a car does not suddenly lurch forward. However, on December
20, 2009, the vehicle that he attempted to extricate from the snow, by pushing it from the rear, lurched forward suddenly, with the
wheels spinning. The driver had accelerated, causing an unexpected and abrupt movement of the car that caused petitioner to

fall and injure his shoulder. Petitioner did not have a pre-existing condition.
Petitioner contends that the incident was undesigned and unexpected; the mere possibility that he could have anticipated
the car lurching forward does not preclude the incident from being an undesigned and unexpected traumatic event. Respondent
contends that the incident was foreseeable and simply the result of strenuous work effort, which is insufficient to render it
undesigned and unexpected.
LEGAL ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSION
In order to qualify for accidental disability retirement benefits, a member of the PFRS must be permanently and totally disabled
as a direct result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his or her regular or assigned duties.
N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. In Richardson v. Board of Trustees, PFRS, 192 N.J. 189 (2007), the New Jersey Supreme Court set the
current standard for accidental disability benefits, whereby a member who has demonstrated permanent and total disability must
1
also prove, in pertinent part, that the disability is
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and unexpected, and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease
that is aggravated or accelerated by the work).
[192 N.J. at 212–13.]
The Court stated that “a member who is injured as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap has satisfied the
traumatic event standard.” Id. at 213. It gave the examples of a police officer who suffers a total and permanent disability from a
fall while chasing a suspect, or a gym teacher who “trips over a riser and is injured.” Ibid. The Court emphasized that a traumatic
event can occur during ordinary work effort in the course of regular or assigned duties. By way of example, “[a] policeman can be
shot while pursuing a suspect; a librarian can be hit by a falling bookshelf while re-shelving books; a social worker can catch her
hand in the car door while transporting a child to court,” and each scenario is “undesigned and unexpected.” Id. at 214.
The polestar of the inquiry is whether, during the regular performance of his job, an unexpected
happening, not the result of pre-existing disease alone or in combination with the work, has occurred
and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability of the member.
[Ibid.]
In Brooks v. Board of Trustees, Public Employees’ Retirement System, 425 N.J. Super. 277 (App. Div. 2012), cited by
petitioner, the court further explained the Richardson tests, particularly the requirement that a work-connected event must be
“undesigned and unexpected” to constitute a “traumatic event.” In Brooks, a school custodian was injured when he attempted to

support one end of a heavy weight bench after students, who had been carrying the other end, suddenly dropped it, causing
disabling injuries to the custodian’s shoulder. The administrative law judge (ALJ) and the Board found that the event was not
“undesigned and unexpected,” reasoning that the custodian should have anticipated that such an event could have occurred and
that he was negligent by not taking action to avoid this foreseeable event. The court held that an accident can be “undesigned
and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in retrospect that the employee could have
anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to avoid it. Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284. And an applicant’s
“simple negligence” that is a contributing cause to the incident, as opposed to “willful negligence,” is not a disqualifying factor.
The applicant need only show a “total and permanently disabling injury ‘as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated
mishap.’” Id. at 284–85 (quoting Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213).
In the unreported decision of Onesti v. Board of Trustees, PFRS, No. A-2791-11 (App. Div. March 27, 2013),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, a police officer injured his hand while using a staple gun to reattach a paper target
during a firearms-qualification test. The Board denied accidental disability benefits on the grounds that the disability was not the
result of a traumatic event, as the incident was not “undesigned and unexpected,” and the disability was the “result of his willful
negligence.” The Board subsequently rejected the ALJ’s determination that the incident was an accident that produced “a totally
unexpected consequence,” and concluded instead that petitioner’s own negligence in failing to examine the staple gun made his
injury “reasonably foreseeable and thus not undesigned and unexpected.” The court reversed and remanded the matter to the
Board for reconsideration in light of the Brooks decision, which had been reported while the case was on appeal.
Here, the Board argues that the injury did not result from an undesigned and unexpected event because it was a
foreseeable consequence of a routine task, and was at best the result of strenuous work effort. The Board cites Cattani v. Board
of Trustees, PFRS, 69 N.J. 578 (1976), as support for the proposition that strenuous work effort does not constitute an
undesigned and unexpected traumatic event. However, in Cattani, accidental disability benefits were denied to a firefighter who
had heart disease and was disabled when he performed unusually strenuous firefighting activity, because aggravation of a pre-
existing condition was not a traumatic event regardless of whether the work effort was usual or unusual.
This matter does not involve any contributing prior medical condition or extraordinary work effort, as in Cattani. Here,
there indeed was an external traumatic event without any aggravation of pre-existing illness. Rather, petitioner responded in the
course of his duties to assist someone who had a medical appointment in freeing her car from the snow. He pushed the car from
the rear, and it lurched forward suddenly, with the wheels spinning. The driver had accelerated, causing an unexpected and
abrupt movement of the car that caused petitioner to fall and injure his shoulder. Indeed, the event was an “‘identifiable,
unanticipated mishap.’” Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284–85 (quoting Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213).
Simply put, “during the regular performance of his job, an unexpected happening, not the result of pre-existing disease
alone or in combination with the work, has occurred and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability of the member.”
Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 214. As stated in Brooks:
The ALJ, whose recommended decision the Board adopted, reasoned that because appellant took
charge of carrying the weight bench into the gymnasium with the assistance of the students, he
should have anticipated the dangers involved in this work, including the risk that the bench would fall
on his foot, and therefore, his accident was not “undesigned and unexpected.” However, it could as
well be said that a librarian who re-shelves books should reasonably anticipate that if this activity is
not conducted properly, the book shelf could fall, that a social worker who transports a child to court
should anticipate that if she is not careful getting into or out of her car, she could catch her hand in
the car door, and that a gym teacher who does not look at the ground while walking should anticipate
that he or she could trip on a riser or other object. Yet the Court recognized that such work-
connected accidents could constitute “traumatic events.” Thus, it is clear that an accident can be
“undesigned and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in
retrospect that the employee could have anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to
avoid it.

[Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 284.]
See also Minosse v. Bd. of Trs., PFRS, TYP 8553-11, Initial Decision (January 4, 2012), adopted, Bd. of Trs. (February 14,
2012), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/> (traumatic event was undesigned and unexpected where police officer was
injured when he kicked open a barricaded door and struggled with a suspect after being dispatched to a domestic-violence
location). Therefore, the potential foreseeable consequence of the occurrence does not make it undesigned and unexpected.
Accordingly, under the facts and circumstances presented here, I CONCLUDE that petitioner’s disability directly resulted
from a traumatic event that was undesigned and unexpected and, as all of the other requisite criteria have been met, his
application for an accidental disability pension should be approved.
DECISION AND ORDER
Therefore, the decision of the PFRS Board to deny petitioner’s application for accidental disability retirement benefits is
hereby REVERSED. I ORDER that petitioner’s application for accidental disability benefits be APPROVED.
I hereby FILE my Initial Decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE POLICE AND FIREMEN’S RETIREMENT
SYSTEM for consideration.

State of New Jersey
OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE LAW
INITIAL DECISION
OAL DKT. NO. TYP968-14
AGENCY DKT. NO. 2-10-

Petitioner,
v.
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES’
RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
