Alexander J. Wazeter, Esq., for petitioner (Helmer, Conley, Kasselman, P.A., attorneys)
Jane Lafferty, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (John J. Hoffman, Acting Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: July 17, 2015 Decided: August 24, 2015
BEFORE WILLIAM TODD MILLER, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
3 On October 17, 2013, the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees’ Retirement System (Board or PERS) denied
petitioner’s application for accidental-disability retirement benefits. The Board concluded that petitioner met all requirements for
eligibility under the applicable accidental-disability retirement law except that petitioner’s accident was not undesigned and
unexpected and there was no actual accident or external happening. Petitioner contends that he is eligible for accidental-
disability retirement benefits as a result of seriously injuring his lumbar spine, requiring a multi-level fusion, when he fell on a wet
tile pool deck while he was stepping off bleachers. For the reason discussed below, the determination of the Board is reversed.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY

1
The petitioner requested a hearing, and the matter was filed at the Office of Administrative Law on January 24, 2014, to be
heard as a contested case pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to -15 and N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -13. The matter was heard on
February 17, 2015, and May 26, 2015. Closing briefs were submitted, and the record closed on July 17, 2015.
FACTUAL SUMMARY
The date of the incident is July 13, 2011. Petitioner was fifty-three years old and was employed as a teaching assistant by the
Department of Children and Families (DCF). Petitioner has more than thirty-two years of creditable pension service.
Petitioner’s teaching-assistant duties included, but were not limited to, serving DCF “at-risk” youths in numerous
supervisory capacities. (J-2.) These youths included students from group homes and students with emotional problems.
Petitioner also acted as a gym monitor and supervised detentions.
3 On July 13, 2011, petitioner was assigned to assist in taking DCF students from the Cape May County location to the
Cape May County Special Services School District (Special Services) for a swimming classA. pproximately eighteen students
went to the Special Services indoor pool. A certified swim instructor was present and provided swimming instruction to most of
the students.
A few students refused to swim, and petitioner was assigned to them as an aide. The non-swimming students were
permitted to sit on the bleachers surrounding the pool deck. Petitioner described the bleachers as the old-fashioned wooden
gym bleachers with approximately eight seats or steps up to the top bleacher, which rests against the back wall. Petitioner and
some of the students walked up the bleachers and sat against the back wall while the remaining students were in the pool. The
students were in and out of the pool during the class, causing the pool deck to get wet.
Special Services had a fire drill approximately twenty minutes into the swimming class. The alarm sounded and the
children in the pool exited. Petitioner and his non-swimming students were guided down the bleachers, and the students were
escorted out of the pool area. Petitioner walked down the bleachers behind the students. When he reached the bottom of the
bleachers and placed his first foot on the pool deck, his foot went out from under him and he flipped into the air, landing on his
back. He hit the tile pool deck very hard. Petitioner struck his left pelvic area at around his belt line, and also landed on his
shoulder blade.
The swim instructor apparently heard the impact, and immediately came to petitioner’s assistance. Petitioner was treated
at the scene, but no emergency services were required. Petitioner returned to the DCF building with his students, by bus. He
then was taken to the hospital.
Petitioner was required to prepare a written statement of the incident. (P-1.) The statement provides as follows:
Students were swim-testing at the Special Services School District Pool.I was sitting with students
on bleachers when a fire-drill was executed. I stepped [off] the bleachers onto a wet floor. My feet
went completely out from under me. I landed hard enough to be heard by other staff on my upper left
buttocks and fell back, hitting my back shoulder blade on the bleacher.
Petitioner eventually was diagnosed with considerable injury to his lumbar spine in the area of L-5 through S-1. He underwent

surgery, during which a rod and four screws were inserted into his spine. His L-4, L-5 and S-1 vertebrae were fused together.
Petitioner’s testimony was credible, and reliably established facts that were not disputed by the Board. Therefore, they were
accepted for purposes of this record as the facts of the case.
LEGAL DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
Petitioner filed for accidental-disability retirement benefits pursuant to N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43. This statute provides in
relevant part:
A member who has not attained age 65 shall, upon the application of the head of the department in
which he is employed or upon his own application or the application of one acting in his behalf, be
retired by the board of trustees, if said employee is permanently and totally disabled as a direct
result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or
assigned duties, on an accidental disability allowance.
In Richardson v. Board of Trustees, Police & Firemen’s Retirement System (PFRS), 192 N.J. 189 (2007), the New Jersey
Supreme Court modified the standard to qualify for accidental-disability retirement. To obtain accidental-disability benefits, a
member must prove:
1. that he is permanently and totally disabled;
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and
unexpected,[2]
and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease
that is aggravated or accelerated by the work);
3. that the traumatic event occurred during and as a result of the member’s regular or assigned
[3]
duties;
4. that the disability was not the result of the member’s willful negligence; and
5. that the member is mentally or physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other
duty.

[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13 (emphasis added).]
“Traumatic event” and “accident” are synonymous in the context of accidental-disability law. Id. at 210 (citing Russo v.
Teachers’ Pension & Annuity Fund, 62 N.J. 142, 152 (1973)). Thus, if the term “accident” is substituted for “traumatic event” in
N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43, eligibility is better understood, as the statute would read as follows:
A member who has not attained age 65 shall, upon the application of the head of the department in
which he is employed or upon his own application or the application of one acting in his behalf, be
retired by the board of trustees, if said employee is permanently and totally disabled as a direct
result of [an accident] occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or assigned
duties, on an accidental disability allowance.
The statute does not specify that the incident must have been “undesigned and unexpected,” which was one of the
Board’s stated reasons for denial of accidental disability. This is a judicially created or common-law phrase that has developed
over time as accidental-disability cases have been interpreted over the last forty years. Therefore, the meaning, purpose and
intent of the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” should be understood as the terms are defined and as the court has designed
the phrase to be used, particularly by the illustration provided by the Supreme Court in Richardson.
Richardson holds that a member suffering a career-ending injury that occurs during and as a result of the member’s
regular or assigned duties will be eligible for accidental-disability retirement, so long as the injury does not aggravate a
preexisting condition; the injury was not contrived; and the employee is permanently and totally disabled from the performance of
his usual or any other duty. Richardson provides examples of work-related accidents or mishaps (that occurred during the
member’s regular or assigned duties) that qualify for accidental disability, such as a teacher tripping over a bleacher (as akin to
the present case); a librarian being hit by a falling bookshelf; or a social worker catching her hand in the car door while
transporting a child. Each of these examples demonstrates the Supreme Court’s new vision of the types of work-related
accidents or mishaps that might be eligible for accidental-disability retirement benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213–14.
The Court’s illustrations involve simple accidents or unanticipated mishaps that occur during the member’s work-related
assignments.
By letter dated October 17, 2013, the Board determined that petitioner failed to satisfy the “undesigned and unexpected”
prong (2b) of the “traumatic event” criterion (2) of the Richardson standard, and not the “regular or assigned duties” criterion (3).
The Board’s denial letter to petitioner states, “the event that caused your disability claim is not undesigned or unexpected.” (J-4.)
The Board’s comment suggests or implies that because petitioner was performing his regular or assigned duties and because
“there was no accident or external happening,” petitioner is ineligible for accidental-disability retirement benefits. (J-4.) The
Board holds (and has held) that if the member is performing his regular or assigned duties the incident cannot be undesigned
4
and unexpected. If this were true, no member would ever qualify for accidental disability, because the member must be injured
while performing his regular or assigned duties under Richardson. The Board, in its closing submission, parses or mis-applies
Richardson to the facts of this case and asserts that “work effort itself . . . cannot be the traumatic event.” (Resp’t’s Br. at 13,
quoting Parker-Rogers v. PFRS, No. A-0921-13T1 (App. Div. June 23, 2015), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>.) The
full Richardson quote, in context, provides:
We return again to our case law, which, instead of constituting a single plait, is comprised of two
distinct strands. We denominate the first strand as the Cattani strand. It includes Hillman, Russo,
Cattani, Gerba, Korelnia, and Gable. That strand recognizes the limited purpose underlying the
statutory amendments (to exclude Dwyer and Fattore); declares that, where the disability arises
out of a combination of pre-existing disease and work effort, a traumatic event has not
occurred; underscores that what is required is a force or cause external to the worker (not
pre-existing disease) that directly results in injury; and identifies ordinary mishaps,
including lacerations, trips, and falls, as traumatic events. That strand reaffirms that a

[5]
traumatic event can occur during usual work effort, but that work effort itself or combined with
pre-existing disease cannot be the traumatic event.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 211 (emphasis added).]
Indeed, the Richardson Court supported its decision with specific illustrations depicting how a work-related accident, i.e., work
effort alone, can be the traumatic event.
By way of example, a police officer who has a heart attack while chasing a suspect has not
experienced a traumatic event. In that case, the work effort, alone or in combination with pre-existing
disease, was the cause of the injury. However, the same police officer, permanently and totally
disabled during the chase because of a fall, has suffered a traumatic event. Similarly, the gym
teacher who develops arthritis from the repetitive effects of his work over the years has not suffered
a traumatic event. His disability is the result of degenerative disease and is not related to an event
that is identifiable as to time and place. On the contrary, the same gym teacher who trips over a
riser and is injured has satisfied the standard.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213 (emphasis added).]
The Board’s position has evolved over the last few years, and its decisions seem to be attempting a gradual rewrite or erosion
of the Richardson standard, so that accidents arising from the work effect alone, even without a pre-existing condition, are
excluded from accidental-disability consideration. In my view, such a holding or gradual erosion conflicts with the intent and spirit
of Richardson.
Under Richardson, the member must establish that he was performing his regular or assigned duties in order to qualify for
accidental-disability retirement benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13, criterion 3. Indeed, petitioner here was
performing his school duties by accompanying and supervising the non-swimming students who were sitting in the bleachers. (J-
2.) A fire alarm rang and the students had to be escorted down the bleachers and out of the pool area across a wet tile floor. I
CONCLUDE that petitioner was injured while performing his regular or assigned duties, satisfying Richardson criterion 3, which
the Board does not dispute.
Under Richardson, the member must next establish that while performing his regular or assigned duties, he suffered a
traumatic event. A traumatic event has three elements: (2a) “identifiable as to time and place”; (2b) “undesigned and
unexpected”; and (2c) “caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease that is
aggravated or accelerated by the work).” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. These elements all relate to qualifying the
unanticipated mishap (i.e., accident) for accidental-disability retirement benefits.
The Board here does not challenge prong 2a, “identifiable as to time and place.” The Board does, however, challenge
prongs 2b and 2c, denying accidental disability based on its determination that the event was not “undesigned and unexpected”
and that there was no “external happening.” (J-4.) But an external happening alone is not part of the Richardson criteria or the
statute. The actual language in Richardson states: “2.c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of
pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the work).” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13 (emphasis
added). Thus, the Board misinterprets prong 2c and narrowly construes or limits accidental-disability claims to external events,
ignoring the parenthetical explanation delineating the clear meaning of the term “external to the member.” See Moran, supra, 438
N.J. Super. at 353 (holding, “[w]e conclude that the Board’s decision misread Richardson, misapplied the statute, and took an

unduly narrow view of what constitutes an ‘unexpected and undesigned’ traumatic event”). Clearly, the Richardson Court was
excluding accidents and injuries that involve pre-existing diseases such as arthritis, heart conditions, and degenerative
diseases, and exacerbation of pre-existing injuries. The Richardson Court also made clear that ordinary accidents (e.g.,
“unanticipated mishaps,” as unmistakably explained by the Court) that occur on the job are eligible for accidental-disability
benefits. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213. Here, the Board transposed “caused by a circumstance external to the member”
with “external happening.” (J-4.) Indeed, the Richardson Court was, under prong 2c, limiting accidental-disability benefits when
the accident was due to “pre-existing disease that is aggravated or accelerated by the work.” Richardson did not hold that an
accident had to involve an “external happening,” as used by the Board and in some unreported appellate cases. Richardson
articulated a simple standard: “[t]hus, a member who is injured as a direct result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap has
satisfied the traumatic event standard.” Ibid. (emphasis added). I CONCLUDE that petitioner was injured in an accident
caused by circumstances external to him, and that the accident was not the result of pre-existing disease that was aggravated or
accelerated by the work, satisfying Richardson prong 2c.
Therefore, petitioner is left only with establishing whether the accident was “undesigned and unexpected.” Richardson,
supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. Here, it is plainly obvious that petitioner experienced an unanticipated mishap when he slipped and
fell on the wet pool deck, during a fire drill, while he was escorting students from the area. These circumstances are equally, if not
more, “unexpected and undesigned” than those of the hypothetical examples noted in Richardson of members who would qualify
for accidental disability (a teacher who trips over a bleacher; a librarian who is hit by a falling bookshelf; or a social worker who
catches her hand in the car door while transporting a child). Petitioner was at significantly greater risk of injury when he stepped
off the bleachers onto a wet pool deck during a fire drill than the clumsy teacher who fell over the bleachers or the inattentive
social worker who closed a car door on her hand. Paradoxically, Richardson holds that the clumsy teacher recovers accidental
disability, while the Board in this case holds that a teacher at greater risk of injury must be denied accidental disability. As will be
more fully discussed below, the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” must be given the meaning intended by the Court in
Richardson. I CONCLUDE that the event suffered by petitioner was undesigned and unexpected, satisfying Richardson prong
2b.
To summarize, petitioner was totally and permanently disabled as a result of an on-the-job accident or “unanticipated
6
mishap” (i.e., traumatic event ) while performing his regular or assigned duties. Petitioner’s injury was caused by circumstances
external to him, and the permanent injury was not the result of pre-existing disease that was aggravated or accelerated by the
work. This is precisely what Richardson requires petitioner to prove, and petitioner has met his burden of proof. I so
CONCLUDE.
Recently reported appellate-court decisions support the above conclusions. In Brooks v. Board of Trustees, PERS, TYP
02426-10 Initial Decision (January 28, 2011), aff’d, Bd. of Trs. (March 17, 2011), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, the
Board, in adopting the administrative law judge (ALJ’s) Initial Decision, reasoned that an accident that results from purposeful or
intentional acts is not undesigned and unexpected. Brooks involved a school custodian moving a 300-pound weight bench with
the help of some students. The bench was suddenly and unexpectedly dropped by the students. The custodian was totally and
permanently injured due to spinal herniation(s).
The ALJ and the Board focused on the member’s job duties, and concluded that since the accident occurred as part of
the member’s normal work activity it had to be designed and expected, and therefore accidental disability must be denied. The
language “normal work activity” was juxtaposed with “undesigned and unexpected” to reach this result. This was not the intended
interpretation envisioned by the Supreme Court in Richardson. Indeed, “undesigned and unexpected” falls under a prong, 2b, of
the “traumatic event” criterion, 2, while “regular or assigned duties” is a separate stand-alone criterion, 3, in Richardson.
Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. These are independent criteria that do not amplify, modify or impact upon each other.
Under the Board’s rationale, the majority of work-related accidents would be excluded from accidental disability, because
accidents generally occur during normal work activities, and all work activity is purposeful, designed and expected. Indeed, the
statute states that the member will “be retired by the board of trustees, if [the] employee is permanently and totally disabled as a

7
direct result of [an accident ] occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or assigned duties, on an
8
accidental disability allowance.” N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43. It is simply the occurrence of an “accident” during work that qualifies for
the disability program. On this point the Richardson Court clearly explained:
In sum, the fact that a member is injured while performing his ordinary duties does not disqualify him
from receiving accidental disability benefits; some injuries sustained during ordinary work effort will
pass muster and others will not. The polestar of the inquiry is whether, during the regular
performance of his job, an unexpected happening, not the result of pre-existing disease alone or
in combination with the work, has occurred and directly resulted in the permanent and total disability
of the member.
X.
In this case, the Board conceded from the beginning that Richardson was permanently and totally
disabled as the direct result of a work-related incident. The only contested issue was whether that
incident constituted a traumatic event. Given the clarified test for traumatic event expressed above
and our discussion of work effort, Richardson satisfied the accidental disability statute. While
performing the regular tasks of his job as a corrections officer, subduing an inmate,
Richardson was thrown to the floor and hyperextended his wrist. As a direct result, he became
permanently and totally disabled. The occurrence was (a) identifiable as to time and place; (b)
unexpected and undesigned; and (c) not caused by a pre-existing condition of Richardson, alone or
in combination with work effort. In short, Richardson suffered a traumatic event.
[Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213–14 (emphasis added).]
The Appellate Division reversed the Board in Brooks. The Appellate Division observed in Brooks that
[t]he ALJ, whose recommended decision the Board adopted, reasoned that because appellant took
charge of carrying the weight bench into the gymnasium with the assistance of the students, he
should have anticipated the dangers involved in this work, including the risk that the bench would fall
on his foot, and therefore, his accident was not “undesigned and unexpected.” However, it could as
well be said that a librarian who re-shelves books should reasonably anticipate that if this activity is
not conducted properly, the book shelf could fall, that a social worker who transports a child to court
should anticipate that if she is not careful getting into or out of her car, she could catch her hand in
the car door, and that a gym teacher who does not look at the ground while walking should anticipate
that he or she could trip on a riser or other object. Yet the Court recognized that such work-
connected accidents could constitute “traumatic events.” Thus, it is clear that an accident can
be “undesigned and unexpected” under the Richardson tests even though it may be concluded in
retrospect that the employee could have anticipated the risk of such an accident and taken steps to
avoid it.
A public employee who is totally and permanently disabled as a direct result of a traumatic event
occurring in the course of employment is disqualified from receiving an accidental disability
pension only if the traumatic event resulted from the “member’s willful negligence.” N.J.S.A.
43:15A-43. Consequently, the fact that an employee’s simple negligence may have been a
contributing cause of an accident is not disqualifying. An applicant for an accidental disability
pension only has to show that he or she suffered a total and permanently disabling injury “as a direct
result of an identifiable, unanticipated mishap,” 192 N.J. at 213, 927 A.2d 543, even though the
employee’s conduct may have contributed to that mishap.
[Brooks v. Bd. of Trs., PERS, 425 N.J. Super. 277, 284–85 (App. Div. 2012) (emphasis added)
(footnote omitted).]

It is abundantly clear from Richardson and Brooks, which are the two reported leading authoritative cases, that a member
who is performing his regular or assigned duties cannot be excluded from accidental-disability consideration merely because he
is performing his “regular or assigned duties.” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212. In fact, the Richardson decision and the
pension statute provide that the incident must occur during the member’s regular or assigned duties to be eligible for an
accidental-disability pension. Ibid.; N.J.S.A. 43:16A-7. And the incident only has to be an “unexpected happening,”
“unanticipated mishap” or “accident” to be a traumatic event. To exclude a member from eligibility because he was performing
his assigned duties is illogical, given the statute’s design and the holdings in Richardson and Brooks.
The Supreme Court did not insert a condition or reservation under the “regular or assigned duties” criterion. Richardson,
supra, 192 N.J. at 213. In fact, the hypothetical school teacher and social worker were arguably negligent. And even in cases
where the member is negligent, the member may recover under the accidental-disability pension program according to
Richardson so long as the member was not willfully negligent (i.e., a heightened level of negligence such as deliberately or
recklessly). (See footnote 2); Brooks, supra, 425 N.J. Super. at 285. In 2012, Brooks reaffirmed the notion that ordinary
accidents, “unanticipated mishaps” or “unexpected happenings,” are the legal equivalent of “traumatic events,” and if they occur
during a member’s regular or assigned duties the member is eligible for accidental-disability retirement.
Indeed, “undesigned” and “unexpected” are terms of art that were inserted by the Supreme Court in Richardson. The
words are to be given their intended meaning in the context and structure as presented in that case. And these terms were
inserted specifically under the second prong (2b) of the traumatic-event criterion (2) of the pension standard in Richardson.
These terms deal with whether the member contrived or manufactured his injury. They have no bearing on or relevance to
“regular or assigned duties,” as this term falls under the third criterion (3) of the Richardson pension standard. The Supreme
Court did not intend the phrase “undesigned and unexpected” to be used to modify or explain what is, or is not, part of a
member’s regular or assigned duties. If this was the Court’s intention it would have included these very important terms of art
under criterion 3, and not prong 2b of criterion 2.
“Unexpected” is defined as “happening without warning; not expected.” Black’s Law Dictionary 1667 (9th ed. 2009).
“Undesigned” is defined as “unintentional or not designed.” Collins English Dictionary (2003). The ordinary definitions have no
correlation to job duties. Rather, the ordinary definitions deal with the element of surprise, lack of notice or awareness, shock,
unforeseen or unpredicted happenings. The Supreme Court used “unexpected happening” or “unanticipated mishap” to define
“undesigned and unexpected.” Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 213.
With the assistance of the definitions combined with the Supreme Court’s illustrations, it is apparent that the Supreme
Court intended to deny recovery of accidental disability when the accident was “intentional and designed” (i.e., contrived, part of
the member’s gross neglect), or part of a pre-existing condition, and to authorize accidental-type recovery when the accident
otherwise occurs “without warning.” This is a logical and rational reading of the Richardson Court’s intent based upon the unique
language utilized in Richardson, the organizational structure of the revised paradigm, the clear examples provided therein, and
the recent interpretation by the Appellate Division in Brooks.
The Supreme Court (Richardson) and the Appellate Division (Brooks) have weighed in on this subject with clear guidance in
reported decisions that require no further interpretation. These rulings are binding on the trial courts. I n Jersey City
Redevelopment Agency v. Mack Props. Co. No. 3, 280 N.J. Super. 553, 562 (App. Div. 1995), the Appellate Division stated, “It
is the responsibility of a trial court to comply with the pronouncements of an appellate court. Daniel v. State, Dep’t of Transp.,
239 N.J. Super. 563, 582, 571 A.2d 1329 (App. Div.), certif. denied, 122 N.J. 325, 585 A.2d 343 (1990).” The trial courts have,
in my opinion, embarked on a path to over-complicate Richardson by defining “undesigned and unexpected” outside of its
simple and basic definition.

I am mindful that under the pre-Richardson paradigm, ordinary slip-and-fall injuries and ordinary accidents occurring on
the job were excluded from accidental disability. The member had to establish that the accident resulted from a great rush of
force or uncontrollable power, which eliminated many cases. These proofs made accidental disability much more difficult to
achieve. But the Richardson decision did away with these confusing and arduous requirements, opening up accidental-disability
claims to a multitude of members who are permanently injured from ordinary job-related accidents (e.g., a social worker who
closes a car door on her hand, or a gym teacher who trips over a bleacher).
Richardson ushered in a major course correction in accidental-disability matters. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 210. For
over forty years, the trial courts and appellate courts applied the “great rush of force and uncontrollable power” criteria to define
what a traumatic event was. Hundreds, if not thousands, of cases were heard, denying or granting members eligibility under the
wrong criteria. The Richardson Court sought to clarify and simplify the definition of traumatic event consistent with the legislative
intent.
Post-Richardson, trial courts are confronting the same difficulties as in the pre-Richardson era, but under the new
paradigm with the terminology “undesigned and unexpected.” Almost identical facts and circumstances are being micro-
analyzed and distinguished under razor-thin differences resulting in varied outcomes.
For example, one line of cases involves lifting/pushing accidents. These include a police officer lifting a traffic-control
trailer, a correction officer lifting a paralyzed inmate from his wheelchair, a maintenance worker lifting a weight bench, a
maintenance worker lifting snow while shoveling, a maintenance worker lifting a heavy trash receptacle, and a police officer
pushing a car stranded in the snow. The disposition in all of these cases turns, in part, on the interpretation of “undesigned and
unexpected.”
In Brooks, the Appellate Division held that the member was eligible for accidental-disability benefits when he injured his
back while lifting the weight bench. In Gibson v. PFRS, TYP 16431-12, Initial Decision (November 28, 2014),a ff’d, Bd. of Trs.
(January 13, 2015), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, a police officer was lifting and unhooking a traffic-signage trailer
from the police vehicle when he herniated spinal discs at C5-6 and C6-7. The PFRS Board affirmed the ALJ and approved the
member for accidental disability. In Weinlein v. PFRS, TYP 9736-12, Initial Decision (November 10, 2014),a ff’d, Bd. of Trs.
(December 9, 2014), <http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/>, a police officer injured his left arm and shoulder when, in the
performance of his duties, he pushed a snow-stuck car that lurched forward and caused him to fall. The PFRS Board affirmed
the ALJ and approved the member for accidental disability.
Conversely, in Parker-Rodgers v. PFRS, supra, No. A-0921-13T1 (App. Div. June 23, 2015),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the Appellate Division denied accidental disability where a correction officer lifted a
250-pound inmate out of a wheelchair, injuring his back. The panel determined that it was part of the normal work effort and not
undesigned or unexpected. Likewise, in Ciallella v. Board of Trustees, PERS, No. A-0344-10 (App. Div. July 26, 2011),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the appellate panel held that a sanitation worker who was injured while dumping the
contents of a heavy trash can into a truck was not entitled to accidental disability benefits because the work activity was not
“undesigned and unexpected.” I n Clayton v. PERS, No. A-1098-12T4 (March 28, 2014),
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/courts/>, the panel denied accidental-disability benefits where a maintenance worker
claimed that his disability was due to injuries to his back, legs, and feet as a direct result of a snow-shoveling incident.
All of the aforementioned cases have countless similarities and few differences. The essential and common thread is that
they involve very similar work-related lifting or pushing incidents, resulting in permanent disabilities. A member that lifts a weight

bench or lifts a traffic-signage trailer receives accidental-disability benefits, while a member that lifts an inmate from a
wheelchair or lifts heavy snow while shoveling snow is denied benefits. There is no discernible line of separation. The same
analysis could be made in police/firemen training-exercises cases.
The phrase “undesigned and unexpected” has replaced “great rush of force and uncontrollable power” in presenting a
new quandary for consistently and fairly deciding accidental-disability cases.
If the Board desires to amend or change the accidental-disability standard it must do so through proper rulemaking or
legislation. Metromedia, Inc. v. Dir., Div. of Taxation, 97 N.J. 313 (1984). Trying to amend or modify the Richardson standard
through administrative adjudications that conflict with Richardson denies members proper notice and due process.
I CONCLUDE that petitioner meets the elements of the accidental-disability statute when “accident” is substituted for
“traumatic event.” Petitioner was “permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of [an accident] occurring during and as a
result of the performance of his regular or assigned duties.” N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43.
I further CONCLUDE that petitioner’s lumbar-back injury was “undesigned and unexpected,” as it resulted from petitioner
experiencing an “unexpected happening,” “unanticipated mishap” or “accident” (i.e., traumatic event) that occurred while he was
performing his regular or assigned duties. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 212–13. Stated differently, the injury was not designed
and expected to occur when petitioner was supervising the students at the swimming pool. Petitioner met the Richardson
standard and proved he suffered a career-ending injury that occurred during work-related tasks. The Board cannot use the fact
that the petitioner affirmatively proved that he was performing his regular or assigned duties under Richardson criterion 3, and
thereafter determine that he is ineligible for accidental-disability benefits because he was performing his regular or assigned
duties (holding that accidents that occur during performance of one’s regular or assigned duties are part of the normal work
effort and therefore not undesigned and unexpected). This type of holding is circuitous, and pits the Richardson criteria against
itself (Richardson criterion 3, if proven, negates prong 2b of criterion 2). This is not what Richardson holds or intends, as is so
clearly illustrated by the hypothetical work-related accidents, to wit: a teacher tripping over a bleacher; a librarian being hit by a
falling bookshelf; or a social worker catching her hand in the car door while transporting a child. Each of these examples involves
someone who was performing his or her regular or assigned duties, and because of a work-related accident or unanticipated
mishap that occurred during the performance of those regular or assigned duties, sustained a totally and permanently disabling
career-ending injury that qualified the employee for accidental-disability retirement benefits. The same standard applies to this
petitioner.
ORDER
For the reasons expressed above, I ORDER that the determination of the Board of Trustees of the PERS beR EVERSED.
Petitioner is GRANTED accidental-disability retirement benefits.

_____________________________________
Kathleen Naprstek Cerisano, Esq., for petitioner (Zazzali, Fagella, Nowak, Kleinbaum & Friedman, attorneys)
Kellie L. Keifer-Pushko, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (Paula T. Dow, Attorney General of New Jersey,
attorney)
Record Closed: August 17, 2009 Decided: October 12, 2010
BEFORE CARIDAD F. RIGO, ALJ:

STATEMENT OF THE CASE AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
This matter involves the question of whether monies received by members of the Morris Hills Regional District Education
Association (hereinafter petitioners) for working additional days at the beginning and/or end of the school year should be
considered as compensation creditable towards their pensions.
The matter was initially commenced by a petition filed by the petitioners. The matter was transferred to the Office of
Administrative Law (OAL) and was assigned OAL docket number TYP 03019-06.
On July 26, 2007, I issued an Initial Decision based upon, as agreed by the parties, a joint stipulation of facts, exhibits and briefs.
On September 6, 2007, the Board of Trustees of the Teachers’ Pension and Annuity Fund, hereinafter referred to as respondent,
issued a Final Decision rejecting the Initial Decision and remanding the matter back to the OAL to establish a more complete
factual record by taking testimony.
The remanded matter was assigned OAL docket number TYP 09620-07. Testimony was heard on April 28, and 29, 2009. At the
request of counsel several extensions were given for the submission of closing briefs, and the record closed on August 15,
2009. Due to the inadvertent oversight and voluminous caseload of this judge timely extensions were not obtained.
ISSUE
The issue in this case is whether the monies received by petitioners for their additional work at the beginning and/or end
of the school year should qualify as creditable compensation toward their pensions.
FACTUAL DISCUSSION
The joint stipulation of facts submitted with the motion for summary decision was admitted and marked as exhibit J-1 at the April
28, 2009, hearing, along with exhibits marked J-2 through J-13.
The following is a summary of the testimony of the witnesses.
Robert Weakley
Robert Weakley testified on behalf of the respondent. At the time of his testimony Weakley was employed by the New Jersey
Sports & Exposition Authority as vice president for human resources and labor relations. He had previously been employed as
the Morris Hills Regional District director of educational and administrative services. He was present for and involved in the
negotiations of petitioners’ 2004–2007 Collective Bargaining Agreement (hereinafter CBA).
Weakly testified that Article 16-A, Section II, as found on page 22 of the CBA was brought to his attention because he was

asked if the additional time certain teachers and/or professionals put in was considered pensionable time. It was Weakly’s
opinion that it was not pensionable. He said that according to New Jersey statutes and regulations, pensionable time was an
employee’s base salary and years of service plus education. He said teachers were paid for coaching, extracurricular activities,
clubs, etc.; however, the pay they received for these things was not included in their base salaries and therefore was not
pensionable.
Peter Lazzaro
Peter Lazzaro is a member of the Morris Hills Regional District Education Association, and he testified on behalf of the
petitioners. Lazzaro has worked for the Morris Hills Regional District for twenty-three years.H e is a teacher, guidance counselor
and coach. He has held numerous positions within the Association. He said that as a guidance counselor he worked five
additional days, but those days did not count towards his pension. He said that management required that he and other
members of the guidance staff work those extra five days.
Lazzaro said that consulting teachers were not included in the 2004–2007 CBA because the parties forgot to include
them. According to Lazzaro the omission was an error. These individuals had not been negotiated out of the contract. Lazzaro
testified that after the 2004–2007 contract was signed, in February 2005, he met with Weakly to discuss the omission. He and
Weakley drew up a side agreement to restore the language accidentally omitted. The side agreement was signed by the parties
on February 2, 2005. He said that the 2001–2004 contract had included the extra days as creditable towards the members’
pensions.
Lazzaro testified that Weakley insisted that the language used in the side agreement was not to be construed to say that
respondent agreed that such payment is or is not pensionable. Lazzara said that the question as to what salary is credited
towards the pension is ultimately answered by the Division of Pensions and the courts.
He said the teachers all knew that they had to work those extra days; there was no doubt about it, they knew it was
mandatory.
Lazzaro said that payment for the additional time is considered a stipend, and it is given in a separate check.
Deborah Stuby
Deborah Stuby has been employed by the Morris Hills Regional District as a guidance counselor for twenty-four years.
Her duties have included enrolling students, holding reinstatement hearings, career planning, college-application processing and
advanced-placement testing.
Ms. Stuby testified that the classroom teachers work 183 days; however, her work year is longer by five days. She works
three additional days at the beginning of the school year and two additional days at the end of the school year. Stuby said she
has never been given a choice to work or not work those additional five days. Her supervisor and principal tell her when she has
to put in those extra five days. She looks at it as mandatory, as per the contract. She considers her work year 188 days, not 183.

Yvonne Hourihan
Yvonne Hourihan is a Morris Hills Regional District guidance counselor. She started at the district in 1982 as a teacher,
and later became a guidance counselor. She testified that the end of the school year is always “crunch time.” She has to work
the additional time so that all of the work can get done. She considers it mandatory, as per the contract.
Barbara Lehmann
Barbara Lehmann has been the Morris Hills Regional District’s social worker for twenty-two years.A s a member of the
District’s child study team she evaluates students and completes individual plans. She also works with new students coming into
the District. She has worked extra days every summer for the last twenty-two years. She routinely works three additional days in
July and August. She gets the students’ files after school ends for the year, generally after July 1. She considers that she works
186 days. She stated that she has no choice but to work the additional days.
Theresa Wisolmerski
Theresa Wisolmerski is a learning disabilities teacher consultant for the Morris Hills Regional District, and has worked for the
District for seven years. She is the case manager for fifty students. She does the testing for students, she runs an extended-year
program, and she has a large number of autistic and severely physically impaired students. She basically deals with classified
students. Wilsolmerski said she actually works a lot more than the three additional days required in the contract. Wilsolmerski
said she has no choice, she must work those three additional days.
FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
I FIND that the petitioners employed by the Morris Hills Regional District are required by contract to work additional days beyond
the normal 183 days. Exhibit J-2, Section II, Article 16 (A)(2).T he individuals who testified for the Association all said that they
considered the additional days as mandated by their contract with the school district.
I FIND that these members work the additional days after the school year has ended and/or before the start of the school year
because of the nature of their work. Their work requires them to either begin or conclude their duties either before or after the
school year. Their work is ongoing, it is neither temporary nor extracurricular. The duties assigned to these members are not
temporary; the work the members do is a permanent part and an integral function of their job.
N.J.S.A. 18A:66-2(d) does not exclude from pension credit compensation for the temporary performance of permanent duties; it
only excludes additional remuneration for the performance of temporary or extracurricular duties. See Siri v. Board of Trustees,
262 N.J. Super. 147 (App. Div. 1993). The work to be excluded is work that by its nature is temporary or extracurricular. There is
nothing temporary or extracurricular about the work these petitioners do. They must perform certain duties outside of the regular
school days in order for the programs or curriculum they are responsible for to function properly and effectively. The fact that the
days these teachers have to work are not specified as to dates and time is not enough to convert their job duties to temporary
status.

Therefore, I REAFFIRMm y prior conclusion in TYP 03019-06 that petitioners have met the requirements of N.J.S.A. 18A:66-
2(d) with regard to the compensation they have been earning for working the additional days in their positions of guidance
counselor, child study team member, student assistant coordinator and English as a second language teacher.
ORDER
It is therefore ORDERED that the Board of Trustees of the Teachers’ Pension and Annuity Fund grant these members the right
to acquire pension credit retroactively for the contract period of July 1, 2004, through June 30, 2007.

limit is otherwise extended, this recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B 10.

INITIAL DECISION

AGENCY DKT. NO. PERS 2-10-225355
JAMES HENDERSON,
Petitioner,
v.
BOARD OF TRUSTEES, PUBLIC
EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM,
Respondent.
___________________________
Frank M. Crivelli, Esq., for petitioner (Pellettieri, Rabstein & Altman, attorneys)

Danielle P. Bradus, Deputy Attorney General, for respondent (Anne Milgram, Attorney General of New Jersey, attorney)
Record Closed: December 17, 2008 Decided: May 5, 2009
BEFORE LISA JAMES-BEAVERS, ALJ:
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
Petitioner James Henderson appeals from the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees' Retirement System's (PERS) denial of his application for
accidental disability retirement benefits pursuant to N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43. Henderson sustained injuries on his job in two separate incidents.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On June 25, 2007, Henderson filed an application for accidental disability retirement. On November 8, 2007, the PERS Board denied his
application, but granted him ordinary disability retirement benefits, agreeing that he was permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of the
incidents that occurred on April 7, 2003, and June 13, 2006. It set forth that the indent of June 13, 2006, was not a "traumatic event" as defined in
N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43 and relevant case law. On December 17, 2007, Henderson appealed the Board's determination and asked that the matter be
deemed a contested case and referred to the New Jersey Office of Administrative Law (OAL) for hearing pursuant to N.J.S.A. 52:14B-1 to -13
and N.J.S.A. 52:14F-1 to -15. On February 21, 2008, the Board transmitted the case to the OAL, where it was filed on March 4, 2008. The
case was heard on November 14 and 17, 2008. The Board moved for summary dismissal after Henderson presented his case. The motion was
denied. The record was held open for the receipt of closing arguments. The record closed on December 17, 2008. The decision was filed pursuant
to an extension to file an answer.
STIPULATED FACTS
The parties stipulated to the following facts:
1. Petitioner, James Henderson, was born on July 5, 1961.
2. Petitioner began work for Princeton Regional Schools in Mercer County as a maintenance tech on July 1, 1990.
3. Petitioner was injured when he was pinned between a sport utility vehicle (SUV) and a snow blower on April 7, 2003.
4. Petitioner was injured when he removed an access panel from the compressor compartment of an air conditioning unit on June 13,
2006.
5. Petitioner filed an application for accidental disability retirement with an effective date of July 1, 2007.
6. At the time petitioner filed his application for accidental disability he was employed as a supervisor of buildings and grounds.
7. On November 7, 2007, the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees' retirement System determined that although petitioner was
permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of the incidents that occurred on April 7, 2003, and June 13, 2006, the incident of June
13, 2006, was not considered a "traumatic event" as described by N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43 and the relevant case law. The basis for the
Board's denial of accidental disability is that the incident of June 13, 2006, was not undesigned and unexpected and the event was not
caused by an external circumstance.
8. On December 17, 2007, petitioner appealed the November 7, 2007, determination of the PERS Board and requested an administrative
hearing.
9. On February 21, 2008, the PERS Board approved the petitioner's request for a hearing and the matter was transferred to the Office of
Administrative Law as a contested case.
FACTS
The following facts are, for the most part, not in dispute. Petitioner, James Henderson, began work as a maintenance technician in the
Princeton Regional School District in 1990. As such, he was required to and did enroll in the PERS. He left Princeton and went to work for the
Mercer County Special Services School District (MCSSSD) as supervisor of buildings and grounds in December 1999. The MCSSSD consisted
of five buildings that it owned. He was required to prepare purchase orders and requisitions, supervise custodial staff and maintain the physical
plant.
On April 7, 2003, while using a snow blower in the school parking lot—one of his regular and assigned duties—he was struck by an SUV
and pinned between it and the snow blower. The accident pushed his spine forward and caused serious injury and pain to his lower and mid back.
He was taken to the emergency room at Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital. Through Worker's Compensation, he was referred to

Dr. Marc Levine at Trenton Orthopedic Group. After x-rays, an MRI and a CT scan were performed on his spine, it was determined that
Henderson had spondylolisthesis and bulging discs in the spine. Henderson underwent physical therapy, supervised by Dr. Levine. Dr. Levine
recommended surgery when Henderson was not improving with physical therapy. Henderson declined surgery, despite Dr. Levine's warning that
without surgery his condition would likely deteriorate. Henderson remained out of work for a significant amount of time. He could not say exactly
how long.
Henderson returned to work on light-duty restrictions as he continued to experience pain. He experienced a tremendous amount of pain in
his back and down his left leg. He also had neck pain and headaches. In July 2003 he returned to full duty performing all the duties as supervisor of
buildings and grounds, except that he would not do heavy lifting such as off-loading trucks. He returned to work because he is the sole provider for
his family of four, which includes two special needs children. If his pain flared up, he would walk it off.
On June 13, 2006, Henderson injured his back at work a second time while repairing an air conditioning unit. At that time, he was still in
daily, continuous pain. He had no intervening accidents between the 2003 accident and the 2006 incident. On June 13, 2006, he went to fix the air
conditioner in a classroom that was having temperature control problems. There is a panel on the air conditioning unit that is two feet by two feet.
He removed the screws and took it off. When he turned slightly to set the unit down, he immediately felt a click in his low back and experienced a
sharp pain. He estimates that the unit weighed between fifteen and twenty pounds. He kept working that day and finished the day, although he was
in pain.
Henderson testified that his pain increased when he went home and through the night. He woke up and noticed increased pain and stiffness.
He went to work approximately three more days, but the pain increased. He told his secretary he "tweaked" his back. When he realized that the
pain was not going away, he saw his doctor at occupational therapy, who examined him, gave him pain medication, muscle relaxants and anti-
inflammatory medicines. He testified that, after the June 2006 injury, his pain was in the same parts of his body, but it increased. Eventually, he was
referred back to Dr. Levine. He again underwent physical therapy. After requesting a second opinion from Dr. Tydings, Henderson underwent
spinal-fusion surgery, post-operative physical therapy and rehabilitation. Henderson did not return to work. On June 25, 2007, he filed an
application with the PERS for accidental disability retirement, which was denied.
Dr. David Weiss, after being qualified as an expert in orthopedic medicine, testified for Henderson that he examined Henderson on
September 23, 2008. In addition, Dr. Weiss reviewed Henderson's extensive medical history and the results from the many tests that he
underwent. Henderson's history revealed no evidence of back pain before the 2003 accident. Dr. Weiss testified that the MRI conducted on April
16, 2003, revealed grade 1 spondylolisthesis at L5-S1 and a bulging disc at L5-S1. His report noted that the MRI also revealed a loss of signal
consistent with age-related disc desiccation at L3-L4, L4-L5. The CT scan performed on April 21, 2003, revealed similar disc pathology. He
diagnosed that the 2003 accident had caused traumatic spondylolisthesis.
Dr. Weiss testified that, after the June 2006 injury, which he called a "tortional and axial" injury in which one picks up and twists, he noted
increased pathology indicating an aggravation and acceleration of Henderson's condition. The MRI conducted on June 29, 2006, revealed grade 1
listhesis of L5-S1 secondary to L5 spondolysis, a disc bulge at L3-L4 and disc herniation at L4-L5. The CT scan of October 4, 2006, revealed a
bilateral L5 spondolysis with a grade I spondylolisthesis and disc pathology at L3-L4, L4-L5 and L5-S1. On November 1, 2006, Dr. Tydings
performed complex spinal surgery. He noted that Henderson was to follow up with interventional pain management. Upon complete review, Dr.
Weiss gave the opinion that Henderson was 100 percent disabled in terms of being able to perform his previous employment. The competent
producing factor was the initial event of April 7, 2003, at which time he sustained traumatic spondylolisthesis, and the subsequent aggravation and
acceleration of the lumbar spine pathology in the June 13, 2006, event, which led to the complex surgery and medication of class II opioids.
Dr. Zohar Stark testified that he is board certified in orthopedic surgery. He is licensed in New Jersey with an active practice. He has been
qualified as an expert in orthopedics in other court proceedings. On August 21, 2007, he examined Henderson for approximately thirty to forty
minutes. He reviewed Henderson's history, along with medical reports, Henderson's job description, and Dr. Weiss' report, and began the
examination. The history that he reviewed is consistent with the stipulated facts. Henderson described numbness in the hands and lower back. He
denied having any lower back pain, but said that the pain radiated. He had a regular examination, but had a hard time getting up from the
examination table. He walked with a limp. Dr. Stark testified that in his opinion Henderson was disabled because of degenerative disease of the
lower back and the injury sustained on June 13, 2006. The places that he had injured in the first accident were the same places in which he had
injury after the second. The second accident put him over the edge. He agreed with Dr. Weiss' diagnosis and conclusion and shares his opinion.
The prior records from Henderson's treating physicians referenced degenerative changes. The accident did not cause spondylolisthesis. He testified
that, in summary, the disability is caused by degeneration coupled with the injuries sustained in June 2006 and April 2003.
On cross-examination, Dr. Stark agreed that, in the part of his report in which he gives his assessment, he did not mention degenerative disc
disease. Rather, he said that the disability is directly related to the accidents. However, he testified that his diagnosis was degenerative disc disease
from the accident of April 2003. Henderson's disability is a result of the June 6, 2006, accident that put him over the edge.
I FIND that Henderson's injury from the April 2003 accident was aggravated and accelerated by the June 2006 accident in which Henderson, in
attempting to perform an ordinary task, incurred an extraordinary consequence, leaving him permanently disabled.

LEGAL ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
The issue in this case is whether Henderson is eligible for accidental disability retirement when he suffered an injury in an accident deemed to be a
"traumatic event," returned to work, and then suffered a second injury rendering him permanently and totally disabled. The Board does not dispute
that the 2003 accident is considered a "traumatic event." Henderson must prove his eligibility by a preponderance of the evidence. Atkinson v.
Parsekian, 37 N.J. 143 (1962); In re Polk, 90 N.J. 550 (1982).
N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43 sets forth that, in order to be eligible for accidental disability retirement under the PERS, a member must be
"permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of a traumatic event occurring during and as a result of the performance of his regular or
assigned duties." The statute exempts from coverage disabilities caused by cardiovascular, pulmonary, musculo-skeletal conditions that are not
directly caused by traumatic events arising from the performance of job duties.
The New Jersey Supreme Court in Richardson v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen's Retirement System, 192 N.J. 189, 212-13
(2007), interpreted the "traumatic event" language of N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43 as meaning that an applicant for accidental disability retirement benefits
must prove:
1. that he is permanently and totally disabled;
2. as a direct result of a traumatic event that is
a. identifiable as to time and place,
b. undesigned and unexpected, and
c. caused by a circumstance external to the member (not the result of pre-existing disease that is aggravated
or accelerated by the work);
3. that the traumatic event occurred during and as a result of the member's regular or assigned duties;
4. that the disability was not the result of the member's willful negligence; an [sic]
5. that the member is mentally or physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other duty.
Henderson is permanently and totally disabled from events occurring during and as a result of his regular duties without any negligence on
his part and he is physically incapacitated from performing his usual or any other duty. Therefore, he meets the first, third, fourth and fifth prongs of
Richardson. The second prong of the Richardson standard is in issue in the present case. The Board denied accidental disability benefits on the
grounds that Henderson's permanent disability results from the back injury he suffered while repairing the air conditioning unit in 2006, which it
claims does not meet the "traumatic event" standard because it was not undesigned, unexpected or caused by an external circumstance. Rather, the
Board contends that Henderson's disability is the result of preexisting disease aggravated by work. Thus, the Board argues that petitioner's
disability is an ordinary disability because it is not the "direct result of a traumatic event," but instead is the result of a preexisting disease.
In Richardson, the Court reviewed the Legislative history of the accidental disability statute at issue. Richardson, supra, 192 N.J. at 199. It
noted that, in the 1964 amendments, the Legislature removed the term "accident" and expressly excluded any cardiovascular, pulmonary or
musculoskeletal conditions that were not a direct result of a traumatic event from coverage under the statute. Id. at 199-200. By those changes, the
Legislature made it clear that a preexisting disease or condition plus work effort would not qualify as an accident under the accidental disability
statute. Ibid. As stated in Richardson:
In purpose and in effect, the Legislature rolled back Fattore and returned the definition of accident for pension
statutes to its well-established meaning by excluding the category of "pre-existing disease plus work effort" and
renaming all that remained a "traumatic event." The renaming was necessary to assure that the broadened workers'
compensation definition of accident would not creep back into accidental disability jurisprudence. Thus, the
meaning of traumatic event for accidental disability purposes (what we formerly called "accident") remained "an
untoward event or mishap" that directly caused the member's permanent and total disability.
[Id. at 200.]
The Richardson Court also cited Cattani v. Board of Trustees, Police & Fireman's Retirement System, 69 N.J. 578, 584 (1976), in which
it reviewed the denial of accidental disability benefits to a member who was disabled when he performed unusually strenuous firefighting activity
that accelerated his pre-existing heart disease. Richardson, 192 N.J. at 202. In Cattani, the Board had held that the firefighter had not experienced
a traumatic event and that his condition was the result of his pre-existing disease, and the Appellate Division reversed on the ground that the
unusual and excessive work effort was the traumatic event. The New Jersey Supreme Court rejected the Appellate Division's analysis because "the
aggravation of pre-existing disease by any kind of work effort, usual or unusual, was not intended by the Legislature to be considered a traumatic
event." Ibid. The Court reiterated from an earlier determination that the statute requires a happening external to the worker (not pre-existing
disease alone or in combination with work) to warrant accidental disability benefits.
The phrase "traumatic event" would ordinarily involve a mishap or accident involving the application of some
kind of external force to the body or the violent exposure of the body to some external force.

We recognize that the foregoing definition may not be all-inclusive and that a traumatic event may possibly be
found in some situations which do not literally fall within the external force or violence concept . . . . [However,
W]here, as here, the disability is the end result of a pre-existing cardiovascular condition, work effort alone
whether unusual or excessive, cannot be considered a traumatic event, even though it may have aggravated or
accelerated the pre-existing disease. However, a basis for an accidental disability pension would exist if it were
shown that the disability directly resulted from the combined effect of a traumatic event and a pre-existing disease.
[Ibid. (quoting Cattani, supra, 69 N.J. at 586.]
The limited purpose of the 1964 amendments to the accidental disability statute was to reject the broadened causation standard of
workers' compensation by specifically excepting from the definition of "traumatic event" work effort itself that aggravated or accelerated pre-
existing disease. As explained by the Court in Richardson, "a traumatic event is essentially the same as what we historically understood an accident
to be—an unexpected external happening that directly causes injury and is not the result of pre-existing disease alone or in combination with work
effort." Id. at 212. Accidental disability is therefore properly denied where an employee has a permanent disability resulting solely from a
preexisting organic condition such as cardiovascular disease or a degenerative disease such as arthritis in combination with the ordinary stress or
strain of work because there was no accident, that is, no "traumatic event" that is the direct cause of the disability.
In the present case, petitioner had no preexisting disease; he suffered an injury as a result of a "traumatic event" in April 2003, but his
permanent disability did not manifest immediately. The permanent disability did not manifest until the April 2003 injury was aggravated and
accelerated by the incident of June 2006. Henderson and the Board disagree as to whether the June 2006 incident was a "traumatic event." The
second prong of Richardson requires the event be "identifiable as to time and place." There is no dispute that it is. The first dispute is to whether the
event was "undesigned and unexpected" as a matter of law. Henderson, in trying to fix the air conditioner, lifted and removed the access panel from
the compressor compartment of an air conditioning unit that weighed between fifteen and twenty pounds and turned to set it down. He immediately
experienced pain in his lower back that radiated into his leg.
Citing its earlier decision in Russo v. Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund, 62 N.J. 142 (1973), the Richardson Court provided guidance
as to the meaning of undesigned and unexpected. Drawing from cases interpreting insurance policies in accidental death benefit cases, the Russo
Court stated,
In those cases, we concluded that when an insurance policy does not purport to cover an unexpected injury as
such, there must be something about the preceding acts and events, alone or in the light of the unexpected injurious
result, to lead an ordinary person to call the means "accidental," even though, strictly speaking, nothing unexpected
or unforeseen occurred in the course of the preceding acts. In ordinary parlance, an accident may be found either in
an unintended external event or in an unanticipated consequence of an intended external event if that consequence is
extraordinary or unusual in common experience. Injury by ordinary work effort or strain to a diseased heart,
although unexpected by the individual afflicted, is not an extraordinary or unusual consequence in common
experience. We are satisfied that disability or death in such circumstances is not accidental within the meaning of a
pension statute when all that appears is that the employee was doing his usual work in the usual way.
[Russo, supra, 62 N.J. at 154 (emphasis added) (citation omitted).]
Similarly, the board adopted the conclusions of the administrative law judge in DiMinno v. Board of Trustees, Police and Firemen's
Retirement System, TYP 1416-07, Initial Decision (December 17, 2007), adopted, Board of Trustees (February 13, 2008)
<http://njlaw.rutgers.edu/collections/oal/search.html>, in which an injury that occurred in the act of a police officer breaking down a door with a
crow bar, an event that was initially considered going about one's usual job in the usual way, was found to be an unexpected and undesigned event
caused by an external circumstance.
In keeping with the Russo analysis, looking at the acts preceding Henderson's 2006 injury, nothing unexpected or unforeseen occurred.
However, Henderson did not expect that the act of lifting and setting down the access panel, which was not of excessive weight, while turning,
would create the injury that it did. Henderson's injury was an unanticipated, extraordinary and unusual consequence of an intended external event.
The external circumstance was the actual lifting and setting down of the panel while turning.
The Board, while not conceding that the 2006 event was undesigned and unexpected and caused by an external circumstance, also
contends that Henderson's injury was not the "direct result" of a traumatic event because he had a preexisting disease. In Titman v. Board of
Trustees, Teachers' Pension and Annuity Fund, 107 N.J. Super. 244, 247 (App. Div. 1969), the Appellate Division defined "direct result" as
follows:
The word "direct" connotes relative freedom from remoteness, whether in terms of time, intervention of other
contributive causes or the like, or a combination of such factors. The criterion cannot be reduced to a formula
which will solve all cases. The matter is one essentially of degree.
In Titman, a teacher suffered two work-related injuries. In 1960 she injured her left knee after a jump-roping accident during a physical
education class she was teaching. Consequently, she favored her left knee after the accident. Then in 1966, her right leg collapsed while walking
down the stairs at work. The medical proofs indicated that the process that had caused the degeneration of the left knee also eventually affected
the right. Assuming the first incident qualified as a traumatic event, the appellate court explained that:
Here, the disability of the left leg produced no disability to work at [her] assigned duties. It was only the

intervention of a similar condition in the right leg, over six years later, not itself the result of a traumatic event, which
produced plaintiff's disability . . . . The Board here found, on adequate proofs, that the plaintiff's disability resulted
primarily from a progressive disease, and there is no medical proof that the 1960 injury caused that disease.
[Titman, supra, 107 N.J. Super. at 247 (emphasis added).]
Thus, the court concluded that the teacher's ultimate total disability was not a "direct" result of the 1960 incident, but that instead it was primarily a
progressive disease that caused her disability.
However, the facts in Still v. Board of Trustees, Public Employees' Retirement System, 144 N.J. Super. 103 (App. Div. 1976), certif.
denied, 73 N.J. 46 (1977), are more similar to those in the present case. In 1965, Still had fallen and sustained an inguinal hernia and possibly
some back pain. Following a relatively short absence from his duties, during which time he underwent a herniorrhaphy, he returned to his normal
work activities without any apparent interruption. Other than the 1965 incident, he was asymptomatic as to back pain until an incident on
December 17, 1971. On that day, while performing the duties of his job, he climbed up on the wheel of a large mechanical sweeping machine, lost
his balance and fell, striking the lumbar portion of his back on a mechanic's workbench approximately four feet high. After the 1971 accident he
had pain in the lumbar portion of his back, for which he received fairly constant medical treatment. He resumed the duties of his employment with
intermittent absences. He could not perform the more strenuous duties. In the spring of 1972, while lifting an 80-pound bag of fertilizer, he felt
extraordinary pain in the same area of his lower back, accompanied by chest pain. He was hospitalized for about ten days, during which time he
was treated for hypertension and osteoarthritis of spine. In April 1973, while operating a 200- to 300-pound mechanical lawnmower, he again felt
increased pain in his back. He obtained medical attention. In both of these instances he was attempting to perform his normal duties.
In Still, the Appellate Division said it was undisputed that the claimant had preexisting osteoarthritis and scoliosis prior to the December 17,
1971, incident, but that they were "without subjective consequence." Still, supra, 144 N.J. Super. at 106. Moreover, the medical opinions
introduced made it eminently clear that the injury suffered in the fall of December 17, 1971, triggered the claimant's progressive (chronic low back
pain) symptoms and it was evident that he was permanently disabled by June 1973. Additionally, the court stated it was obvious that the incidents
that occurred in the spring of 1972 and in April 1973 were "residuals of the exacerbation of the condition and not in any degree the causes
thereof." Ibid. The court found that both the Board's physician and the claimant's treating physician had testified that the claimant's disability was
caused by a combination of the trauma and the preexisting disease, which the court held fit precisely into the Supreme Court's holding in Cattani,
supra, 69 N.J. 578, that a basis for an accidental disability pension exists if it is shown that the disability directly resulted from the combined effect
of a traumatic event and a preexisting disease that was asymptomatic until the accident. Still, supra, 144 N.J. Super. at 106-07 (citing Cattani,
supra, 69 N.J. at 586). In addition, the court found that two subsequent incidents in 1972 and 1973 were effects and not causes of the ongoing
consequences of the combined trauma and disease.
The Still court noted that the accidental disability statute itself recognizes that disability need not follow the accident immediately, as it
provides five years of the original traumatic event for the filing of applications. Indeed, it can be filed after five years
if it can be factually demonstrated to the satisfaction of the board of trustees that the disability is due to the accident
and the filing was not accomplished within the 5-year period due to a delayed manifestation of the disability or to
circumstances beyond the control of the member.
[Id. at 108 (quoting N.J.S.A. 43:15A-43).]
Subsequently, in Gerba v. Board of Trustees, Public Employees' Retirement System, 83 N.J. 174 (1980), the New Jersey Supreme Court
addressed its observation in Cattani relied upon by the court in Still that a basis for accidental disability pension exists if it is shown that the
disability directly resulted from the combined effect of a traumatic event and a preexisting disease. As explained by the Court:
[A]n accidental disability in some circumstances may arise even though an employee is afflicted with an underlying
physical disease bearing causally upon the resulting disability. In such cases, the traumatic event need not be the
sole or exclusive cause of the disability. As long as the traumatic event is the direct cause, i.e., the essential
significant or substantial contributing cause of the disability, it is sufficient to satisfy the statutory standard of an
accidental disability even though it acts in combination with an underlying physical disease.
[Gerba, supra, 83 N.J. at 187.]
Thus, the Court explained that it is not enough that the trauma aggravate or accelerate the prior condition; rather the trauma must be the
"essential significant or substantial cause." Id. at 187-88. In Gerba, the claimant experienced traumatic events, but his disability (arthritis) was not a
direct result of the traumatic events that he experienced. The Court denied recovery to the claimant, finding that the traumatic events he
experienced did not cause his disability, but that his preexisting arthritic condition had. Id. at 188; see also Korelnia v. Board of Trustees, Public
Employees' Retirement System, 83 N.J. 163 (1980).
In Petrucelli v. Board of Trustees, Public Employees' Retirement System, 211 N.J. Super. 280 (App. Div. 1986), a claimant had a
preexisting asymptomatic condition: spondylolisthesis. After a traumatic fall down a staircase, symptoms and accompanying pain commenced,
eventually disabling the claimant. The claimant argued that, even if the court were to find that the spondylolisthesis was involved, it was the
traumatic fall that constituted the "essential significant or substantial contributing cause" of the disability. Id. at 287-88. The court agreed,

concluding that "if [the] claimant here cannot recover after a severe trauma, superimposed on a nonsymptomatic, structural anomaly, which
triggered a symptom complex resulting in total disability, no claimant could ever recover accidental benefits in any circumstance where there exists
a quiescent underlying condition which had caused no trouble and might never [have]." Id. at 289.
In the present case, Henderson's disability was a "direct result" of two traumatic events on April 7, 2003, and June 13, 2006. Henderson
did not have a preexisting disease or condition prior to April 2003. The Richardson Court denied workers from receiving accidental disability as a
result of a preexisting condition. It did not intend for the meaning of "preexisting disease" and "preexisting condition" to encompass those injuries
that were caused by a previous traumatic event. Further, the intent of the Legislature was to provide accidental disability retirement benefits to a
worker permanently and totally disabled as a direct result of an accident occurring in the performance of his duties. To deny Henderson under
these circumstances would be to punish him for returning to work after the first accident when he had no choice but to do so.
Therefore, I CONCLUDE from the medical proofs, testimony and other evidence in the record that Henderson's disability resulted from
the combined effects of the two job-related accidents in April 2003 and June 2006. I further CONCLUDE that the two incidents were "traumatic
events" by statute and under Richardson. Last, I CONCLUDE that as both accidents were traumatic events under the statute, Henderson
qualified for accidental disability benefits.
ORDER
I ORDER that the determination of the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees' Retirement System denying Henderson's application
for accidental disability retirement benefits is REVERSED, and that Henderson's appeal requesting such benefits is GRANTED.
I hereby FILE my initial decision with the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES' RETIREMENT SYSTEM for
consideration.
This recommended decision may be adopted, modified or rejected by the BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE PUBLIC EMPLOYEES'
RETIREMENT SYSTEM, which by law is authorized to make a final decision in this matter. If the Board of Trustees of the Public Employees'

recommended decision shall become a final decision in accordance with N.J.S.A. 52:14B-10.
Within thirteen days from the date on which this recommended decision was mailed to the parties, any party may file written exceptions with the

INITIAL DECISION

Petitioner,
v.
POLICE AND FIREMEN'S RETIREMENT
SYSTEM,
